Regarding the Chan Master Nan of the Arhats:
his name was Xinan. He was born into the Zhang family in Tingzhou. Having left home at a young age, he received the full precepts under the guidance of Jinquan Temple.

He was pure and simple in nature, with lofty principles and high aspirations. Having traveled through various monasteries, he went to consult Chan Master Yunju You, whereupon he realized the mind-ground.
Having received the master’s final entrustment, he intended to travel once more to seek instruction from masters throughout the land.

At that time, Chan Master Fakuang Zhaojue—a fellow disciple of Yunju—was propagating the Dharma at Donglin, and his school was particularly flourishing. The Master went to visit him, and Zhaojue knew of his coming in advance.
Upon his arrival, he struck the great bronze bell and gathered five thousand disciples. He went out to welcome them beyond Tiger Creek;

from this, the Master’s reputation flourished and his influence grew weighty in the world. Before long, the Governor of Nankang appointed him to the abbacy at Luohan Monastery, where he succeeded to the Dharma of Yunju.
His spiritual prestige became renowned throughout the land, and students called him "Little Nan. A monk asked: "When sound and form do not reach [the mind]..."
"The illness lies in seeing and hearing; words cannot reach it. The fault rests with the lips. This one principle and two meanings—please, Master, point directly.
The Master said, "A single character does not bear a stroke. [The student] said, "The clear waters of the ancient stream welcome the new moon;

the cold plum blossoms on the old ridge meet spring again. The Master said, "Two characters do not form a pair. [The student] said, "At midnight, colored clouds enshroud the jade elephant; at daybreak—"
"The peak is hidden by clouds. The Master said, "What a truly authentic message! Question: "The lion cub follows the herd;
at three years old, it can already let out a great roar. Before it has even left the forest, what is this one phrase? The Master said, "Its head would split and its forehead crack."

[The student] asked, "After emerging from the forest, what is the one phrase? The Master said, "The crown of the head touches the ground. [The student] asked, "When there is neither emerging nor entering, how is it?
The Master said, "Advancing forward and retreating backward. [The student] asked, "Tell me, where does it fall? The Master said, "The assembly has eyes.
Then he said: "The Way is impartial; its power cannot be opposed. It is like the wind passing through grass, which bends down. Like spring...

When the flowers bloom, even the Buddha’s hand cannot shield them; how can the human mind possibly be restrained? To follow this truth, every thing radiates brilliance; to oppose it, every aspect loses its luster.
Neither opposing nor following, one allows the vessel to be square or round as it may. Invocations respond to the sound; high and low arise spontaneously.
Like an image reflected in a mirror, subject and object lose their emotional distinction. What appears is like illusory supernatural power; what is accomplished is like illusory right enlightenment.
Awakened! He directly attained a state where ten thousand layers of Mount Lu together turn the Dharma wheel, and the thousand-fathom waters of the Poyang River jointly proclaim the profound meaning.
It is thus: the golden rooster pecks through the lapis lazuli shell; the jade hare pushes open the gates of the azure sea. It is also said:

The painted horn atop the red pavilion announces the spring dawn; ten thousand households celebrate together as all things are renewed. Who would have known that the green cypress trees at the edge of the courtyard—*bian* (suddenly/then)!?
This is the person who questions the Dharma in this very life: they have no body that can be called a body, and no years that can be called years.

From beginning to end there is no change; coming and going, they are ever-present. Though the four seasons shift, they do not shift; though the single breath moves, it is not movement. A hundred years of birth and death are like drifting clouds;
ten generations of past and present are like a flash of lightning. Their sentiment transcends the realm of forms; their Way accords with the center of the circle. Not even a hair’s breadth exists.
"May your lifespan be equal to that of empty space. Simply, through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, recognize your original face.
Do you see it? The jade hare sinks behind the western ridge; the golden crow emerges from the eastern sea. He also said: "Without relying on a single blow, the great treasure is perfected;
the Great Axe leaves its scabbard, its cold light chilling. For your sake, I have severed the rams' horns and forged an emerald jade platter out of empty space. How excellent!
Pick it up! You must look further still; turning it over and over, it is pitch black. Striking the meditation seat with his whisk, he descended from the seat and said:
"At Mount Tang, today the furnace has been opened; the thin, cold clouds have gathered, yet the snow has not yet fallen.
Stir the fire as you please and discuss its heat and cold; who knows who can call out to the Minister? The ancient sages sought people within hot ashes; this is the practice of all Buddhas.
Within the flames of the Way, one sees at once: in every land and every atom, all are identical to oneself; in every thought and every moment, all are in perfect accord with the fundamental source.
Yet, to understand it in such a way is to turn away from what is appropriate. Why? Because "a single phrase that fits the head" is "the tethering stake for ten thousand kalpas.
It is also said: "Heaven and earth are the furnace and bellows; the sun and moon are the tongs and hammer. Only by smelting the pure wind does one become a Buddha."
Chengzu practiced the White Cloud method with its proper techniques and rituals; a halo encircled his neck and the *svastika* was inscribed upon his chest.
"A-he-he! Do you know or not? Riding backward upon the lion throne, he leaps up to Mount Sumeru! He further said:
"In the ninety days of a summer retreat, day after day there is no deviation; in the twelve hours of a single day, hour after hour there is no difference—just like the yellowness of gold."

The azure of the blue sky—its color and its height remain unchanging and indestructible. To settle upon a single name or attach a single character, how could it possibly resemble my own numinous awakening?

Thus, one cultivates the myriad practices that are like flowers in the sky, dwells in a meditation hall that is like the moon reflected in water, subdues the demonic armies within a mirror, and realizes the fruit of Buddhahood within a dream.
Today, as the year of the Dharma has come to its full term, it is all thoroughly understood.
Do you understand yet? Shifting the body, one shakes the Taihua Peak; cupping the sweat, one sprinkles the *tathāgata-garbha* (*tīpóhú*).
It is further said: "Object and self are both as such; right and wrong are of one breath. The clouds have no mind, yet they listen to the dragon’s roar, filling heaven and earth;

the wind leaves no trace, yet it hears the tiger’s howl, uprooting trees and sounding through the branches. The Way has no root, yet it skillfully responds to all conditions, distinguishing the black-robed from the white-robed. Suddenly—
Yet in a single thought, one merges with wind and clouds; one does not know who is "I. There is no place to go, and no place to stay.
A great laugh, ha ha! Rarely encountered, seldom met. He spoke again: "No Zen, no Way; with this three-inch tongue, I sweep it all away in disorder.
Last night the sun’s orb wafted the fragrance of cassia; this morning in the moon’s cave, *zhicao* mushrooms have sprouted. A ha ha! Ten thousand [times]."
The two pieces of gold are nowhere to be found; a single phrase cuts off all deliberation. All phenomena do not reach one another.

On the day the Master was about to pass away, he appointed two Chan practitioners to establish the Sangha. He ascended the hall and said: "To propagate the Great Dharma, one must rely on the right person.
If you borrow a favorable wind, it is easy to raise the sails and ply the oars. Formerly, a monk asked Zhaozhou: "I have newly entered this forest of monks..."
He requested the Master’s instruction. "Have you finished eating your congee? the Master asked. The monk replied, "I have finished. The Master said, "Go wash your bowl.
At these words, the monk attained great enlightenment. Right now, after the bell has rung and before ascending the hall, everyone eats their congee;

once full, they simply stop. If one can chew it through, it will not obstruct anyone. If one cannot chew it through, then [the obstruction] remains. However, if one can chew it through, it is permitted.
"E! Today this Arhat rides an iron horse backward, ascending Mount Sumeru in reverse; he tramples through the void, leaving not even a trace behind.
Do you all see him? Last night the wind arose in the reed courtyard, wafting the fragrance and blowing down three or five peach trees."
He descended from his seat and returned to the abbot’s quarters, where he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Chan Master Yuantong Min was named Daomin;
he was the son of the Cai family of Xianyou in Xinghua. His mother had dreamed of swallowing a *maṇi* jewel before his birth.
She conceived and gave birth to him. When he was five years old, his feet were unable to walk and his mouth could not speak. His mother carried him to Ximing Temple;
upon seeing a Buddha image, he suddenly stepped onto the ground, joined his palms, and recited "Namo Buddha. He then prostrated himself, which caused great wonder among the people.

Later, while attending the imperial academy in Daliang, he suddenly grew weary of worldly dust and left to rely on Vinaya Master Dexiang of Jingde Temple, where he attained proficiency through the recitation of sutras.
Having received full ordination, he traveled extensively to visit the masters of the Zen school. He remained with Master Zhenru Zhe for the longest period.

Later, hearing of the spiritual reputation of Chan Master Ledu Qian of Lanting, he went to rely upon him. Upon their first meeting, Qian—whom the assembly at Daopei hailed as the "Ancient Buddha Min"—recognized his potential and held him in high esteem.
The Master applied himself to intensive practice; whatever insights he attained, he presented them to Qian, who did not yet grant his approval. One night, while standing in attendance, the Master...
Next, Qian cited the occasion of the World-Honored One holding up a flower and commanded [Yan] Shiyan to offer a response; Yan was not in accord. Thereupon, Yan cast aside all that he had heard.
After some time, while walking in meditation, Qian placed his staff upon his shoulder and sighed deeply, saying, "Do you understand? As Yan Shiyan prepared to respond, Qian struck him.
A short while later, Qian picked up a blade of grass and showed it to him, asking, "What is this? As Yan Shiyan prepared to respond, Qian struck him again.
He shouted again. The Master suddenly attained enlightenment and immediately assumed the gesture of holding a flower, saying, "From now on, I shall no longer doubt this old man’s tongue.
Qian pulled him firmly by the hand and said, "Speak further! Speak further! The Master replied, "Clouds rise upon the South Mountain;
rain falls upon the North Mountain. When the nostrils can speak, there is nowhere to be found. He then prostrated himself, and Qian approved. On another day, Qian said to him, "Mount Lu..."

"Excellently so! Your conditions for maturation lie there. He then took his leave. In the first year of the Jianzhong Jinggu era, he appeared in the world at Guankxi in Jiangxia, and subsequently moved to Yuan Tong on Mount Lu.
Initially, when Chan Master Daoyi founded and reformed Yuan Tong, he had given this instruction upon his deathbed:
"My stupa shall be made of green stone; if the stupa turns red in the future, it means I have returned. When the Master arrived, [the stupa indeed turned red].
At evening, the pagoda turned crimson. Far and near were struck with wonder and sighed in admiration, realizing that the Master was surely the reincarnation of Daoji.

From this point on, the school’s influence flourished to its zenith, and monks flocked to him like clouds gathering or spokes converging at the hub of a wheel. The Master maintained his solitary integrity and ascetic practices until the end of his life.

A monk asked, "What is the matter that transcends the Buddha-dharma? The Master replied, "The water at the head of Pijian Creek flows backward. The monk pressed further, "What about when it is hidden? (The Master remained silent).
"How is it when the shadow is exposed? The Master struck him. The monk continued, "I thank the Master for his response. The Master said, "Blind man!
How do you practice throughout the twelve hours of the day? The Master said, "The wind does not come; the tree does not move. Upon these words, the monk attained realization.
At the beginning of the Zhenghe era, Grand Preceptor Cai Jing petitioned for the master Yuanji to be granted the purple robe.
When Vice Minister Fan Zhixu, formerly a Hanlin Academician, traveled from the capital to Yuzhang and passed through Yuantong Monastery, he remarked during their conversation, "I am old now;
having fallen into the midst of those in purple and gold robes, this matter has somewhat receded. The Master immediately called out, "Academician! Fan responded, "Yes? The Master said, "It is so."
"Not far," [Zhao] Han said. "I hope you will further instruct me. The Master said, "From here to Yuzhang is four stages of travel.
Zhao Han stood there lost in thought. The Master said, "If you see it, you have seen it; if you deliberate over it, you have already missed it. Zhao Han nodded in understanding and was delighted.

When State Councillor Wu Gong Juhou returned to Zhongling with his official insignia, he visited the Master and said, "Recently, when I went to the provincial capital for the examinations, I passed through the 'Gate of Zhaozhou' at Yuan Tong."
He asked Master Nü, "What is the matter of penetrating the barrier? Nü said, "Just go and serve as an official; I have been doing so for over fifty years now.
The Master asked, "Have you ever clearly realized the matter of penetrating the barrier? Mì replied, "Eight times I have passed through it, yet I always maintain mindfulness."
However, he was not yet liberated. The Master raised his fan and said, "Please use this fan. Mi waved the fan. The Master said, "What is there that is not liberated?
Mi was greatly delighted and said, "I pray for the final word. The Master shook the fan twice. Mi said, "Intimate! Intimate!
The Master said, "Eat your own tongue! Peng Gong Rulin, the Imperial Counselor, personally transcribed the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.
He gave it to the Master. The Master held it up and said, "Which of these is the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, and which is the *Sūtra* for the Imperial Counselor?
Peng said, "This one was written by my own hand. The Master said, "That is merely the characters; which one is the sūtra? Peng laughed and said, "In that case, it cannot be obtained.
The Master said, "It appears in the form of a lay official and preaches the Dharma for them. Peng said, "Everyone has their share."
The Master said, "Do not slander the sutras. Peng asked, "How is it so? The Master held up the sutra to show him. Peng clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying, "Ah, wonderful!

The Master said, "And yet you say it cannot be attained. When Minister An of the Xiangguo family was exiled to the south, he visited the Master and said, "In my life I have served as an official, but today I am banished;
I realize that everything from before has been but a dream. The Master said, "Minister..."

"Have you awakened, sir? The Duke replied, "All of this has been inherently present; it is simply that I have not yet attained full clarity. The Master called out, "Minister! The Duke raised his head. The Master said, "It is finished. The Duke said, "I am still hindered by affairs. The Master said, "How many stages from the capital have you traveled to reach here? The Duke said, "Forty-two days. The Master said, "Where were you hindered until now? The Duke laughed and said, "I have gained great benefit. The Master said: [The Master said: "If you can say so, then why did you previously claim you were hindered by affairs? The Duke was speechless. The Master said, "This is the meaning of 'the Way is not far. It is right before your eyes; do not look for it elsewhere. If you seek it elsewhere, you will wander further and further away. The Duke bowed deeply. The Master said, "Do not forget what you have heard today. The Duke departed. Later, he sent a messenger to inquire about the Master’s health. The Master said, "I am ill. The messenger asked, "What illness? The Master replied, "I have a headache. The messenger returned and reported this to the Duke. The Duke sighed and said, "The Master truly possesses the Way. He then composed a poem to express his gratitude: "The Great Way is originally not difficult; Only because people create complications is it hard to see. When the mind is pure, the Way is manifest; When thoughts arise, confusion ensues. I have long known this principle, Yet I failed to recognize it within myself. Today, thanks to the Master's instruction, I have finally attained realization. He then sent a letter to the Master, saying: "I have received your compassionate guidance. My former delusions have been dispelled, and I have found peace. I shall now entrust my family and estate to my son and retire to the mountains to cultivate my practice. The Master replied, "If you wish to leave the world, you must first repay your debts to your parents. Only then may you truly be free. The Duke followed this advice and lived out his remaining years in peace. His reputation spread throughout the realm, and all who heard of it praised him as a man of great virtue. This is recorded as the "Instruction to Minister Li. It is said that those who encounter such a teacher and receive such instruction will surely attain liberation. Do not doubt this. Trust and practice it. Thus it is said: "The Way is not far; Seek it not elsewhere. Right before your eyes— Do not look for it outside. If you can understand this, you have attained the Way. If you cannot, you are merely adding more confusion to your confusion. Be careful. Be careful. Do not let this pass in vain. Respectfully submitted. May there be good fortune. "Directly experience it right now" (The Official asked, "How does one experience it? The Master said, "Day after day, it is the same"). [The Official] joined his palms in reverence and joy.
The Master said, "Simply empty all that exists; do not reify what is non-existent. The Official said, "I am fortunate to have encountered this; I shall not dare forget it.
Zuosi Duxiang asked, "This Dharma cannot be understood through conceptual thought or discrimination. How can one arrive at it? The Master said, "Enter the fire with your whole body."
Dugu said, "Ultimately, how is it? The Master said, "Go straight ahead. Dugu hesitated. The Master said, "Would you like some tea? Dugu said, "I cannot bear it.
The Master said, "Why do you not understand it in this way? Dugu suddenly attained realization and said with a smile, "It is too close!
The Master said, "Eighty thousand miles away! Dugu then spoke a verse: "How can it be conceived? It is a great fire!"
The assembly then departed in this manner, without leaving their respective places. The Master said, "There is still this one remaining.

They all said, "Please point it out directly. The Master said, "Just go in this way; the cauldron is cast of iron. They all said, "Excellent, excellent! Li Du-fu, the Governor of the Nine Rivers, asked:
"When the mind is recognized as empty and still, and suddenly all sensory objects appear before one, what then? The Master—
[Zhaozhou] said, "A spark from a flint burns the body. Shoushan suddenly attained realization and said, "The void has been shattered!
Zhaozhou asked, "Where do you apply yourself? Shoushan snapped his fingers once. Zhaozhou said, "Not like that, yet like that. Shoushan bowed and withdrew.
Zhaozhou’s total mastery was one of great freedom, and he brought many others to awakening. In the winter of the third year, he entrusted the affairs of the monastery to [Shoushan].

Shouhui, a disciple who had attained the Dharma, requested retirement from the court. The court granted his request and issued an edict ordering Shouhui to succeed him in the administrative duties of the monastery.
On the ninth day of the tenth month of winter the following year, he gathered the assembly and spoke this verse: "The clay ox let out a great roar last night;
It startled Mount Sumeru so that it hid the Northern Dipper. North, south, east, and west—nowhere can one find it; I have grasped its nostrils."

He lost his voice. He spoke again, saying: "The Ultimate Way is empty and still; it is utterly detached from the faculties and their objects. Where light and its environment both vanish, the spiritual mechanism is beyond all dependence.
True permanence functions spontaneously; how could it belong to coming or going? Its response is all-pervasive and directionless, existing without fixed rules.

When the sturdy gate is struck and rattled, it is as difficult to penetrate as a flash of lightning. One must have one's thousand eyes opened at once; only then can there be no interval between death and life. From this point on, [the truth] shall be resolved."
"You may bury his entire body; three hundred years hence, Buddhist affairs shall flourish. As he was about to depart, he uttered one phrase that did not fall within the realm of seeing or knowing:
"Half-broken and three-fold shattered—take this well for the sake of rebirth. He struck his knee once with his hand and passed away peacefully.

He had lived in the world for sixty-eight years and sat in meditation for fifty summer retreats. His disciples, honoring his final instructions, enshrined his entire body in a stupa, taking only his sitting mat.

The hair and beard gathered at that time were cremated, and all became *śarīra*. The Prefect reported these matters to the throne, and an imperial edict conferred upon it the title "Stūpa of Wondrous Emptiness" (*Miaokong*).
The Master resided at Yuantong for twelve years, responding to sentient beings according to their capacities and exerting himself for the Dharma with total selflessness.

Nevertheless, he absolutely refused to allow his disciples to record his spoken words. Among his followers, there were some who could not bear to discard them, so they secretly compiled them together. The Master was incorruptible.
The *Zhijie* (Admonition) states: "If you must wish to abandon my long-held aspiration, then thirty years hence you may bring it forth.
When Chan Master Tonghui fulfilled this agreement and brought it out, Left Minister Chen Gongguan read the *xiaocan* (small lecture) and said: [Text follows]
If there were even a doubt the size of a mustard seed, you would treat that spiritual friend with respect and praise; thus, I have composed this preface for him.
Subsequently, both Zhang Gongdeyuan, the Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, and Feng Gongjiuchuan, the Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, both commended these words.
The eulogy says: "It is fitting that Yuantong came to respond to the red pagoda. It is said that three hundred years after his passing, he shall promote the Buddhist work.
Perhaps this was a posthumous composition by someone seeking to glorify him. Why? Because Min had indeed attained thorough enlightenment.
When one is thoroughly enlightened, the myriad transformations share in the same efficacy and all capacities are universally reached; what, then, is not Min? As the former Buddha said: "I am unborn."

It is unborn; it neither exists nor does not exist. Thus, the sages and worthies embrace this convergence: in every speck of dust and in every thought-moment, it is thus. Why limit oneself to three hundred years?
If one must depart and necessarily return after three hundred years, then to be busily occupied within the confines of physical forms—would that not be the way of the Lesser Vehicle?
Furthermore, the boundless oceans of lands are not separated by even a hair’s breadth; ten ages are as a single moment.
If the essential principle of mindfulness is not now being shifted, where does it reside? Master Li Shanglao has recorded these events and publicized their excellence;
however, he has failed to investigate the subtle art of the Gate of the Patriarchs in synthesizing and harmonizing [the teachings]. This must be examined together with his account.
Chan Master Doushuai Zhao, whose name was Huizhao, was the son of the Guo family from Nan’an Commandery. He left home and received full ordination at Liaoshan Monastery.

Having completed his training, he traveled extensively to study under Chan Master Congyue. Congyue had studied under Zhenjing and was highly regarded for his realization; Master Zhao heard of this in advance.
His intent was thus; he subsequently established a hermitage at Shitou. Later, Xue met the attendant Shishuang Su and further obtained Shishuang’s "last word.
He sent a letter to the Master saying: "My former study was not yet proficient; there still remains that 'last word'. The Master replied with a verse:

He never slackened in his progress. He regularly performed prostrations to the Buddha at midnight and used this time for rest and meals, refusing to go against the community.
The monastic centers trusted his sincerity, and local customs were transformed by his teaching. He maintained this single practice for thirty years, remaining unchanging from beginning to end.
In the twelfth month of the fourth year, he passed away on Mount Liangshan.
Master Mingbai Hong:
The Chan Master’s name was Dehong, with the style name Juefan. He was the son of the Yu family of Xinchang in Junzhou. At the age of fourteen, his parents both passed away within the same month;
he then went to rely on Chan Master Jing of Sanfeng as a novice. At nineteen, he sat for the scriptural examination in the Eastern Capital.

According to the old records of Jiatai Wanshou Monastery, Huìhóng was designated as a *dà-sēng* (great monk). Under the guidance of Vinaya Master Xuānmiào, he studied the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* until he reached its profound depths.
He read widely across the classics and histories and possessed extraordinary talent; his poetry brought him renown among the scholar-officials (*jìnshěn*) in the capital.
After some time, he returned south and relied upon Chan Master Zhēnjìng of Guīzōng to investigate the Dharma of the mind. Subsequently, he moved to Lètán, where he remained for seven years.
At the age of [blank] years, he attained the Way of True Purity and departed for Eastern Wu. He traveled through the Yuan and Xiang rivers, where one day he read the *Recorded Sayings of Fenyang*;
this served as a powerful catalyst for his realization, whereby his mind was cleansed and his eloquence became vast and unimpeded.

During the Chongning era, Zhu Shiying of the Xianmu Pavilion invited him to take charge of Beichan Monastery in Linchuan. Previously, the monastery had possessed sixteen scrolls of ancient paintings depicting the Sixteen Arhats (*Ṣoḍaśarāhula*).
One of them had been lost for a long time. When the Master arrived, he mocked him with a poem.

Not long after, the Arhat appeared in a dream to the family where [the robe] was hidden and requested it be returned to the monastery; thus, it was recovered. The world said that the Venerable One returned because he still feared such mockery.
The following year, he retired from his duties to travel to Jinling, where the Transport Commissioner Wu Zhengzhong invited him to reside at Qingliang. Before long—

After one month, he was falsely accused by a mad monk for impersonating another’s name on a Buddhist ordination certificate (*duòdì*). He was implicated in a case of slander and cast into the imperial prison.

After being subjected to rigorous interrogation for a long time, he was convicted of impersonation and dressed in lay clothing (*féngyè*). He traveled to the capital to see the Chancellor Zhāng Wújìn, who presented a special memorial on his behalf so that he might receive ordination and change his current name.
The Grand Marshal Guō Tiānmín submitted a petition granting him the purple robe and the title Bǎojiào Yuánmíng (Precious Enlightenment and Perfect Clarity). From then on...

He was titled the Venerable Jiyin. Not long after, he became close friends with Zhang and Guo. When Zhang retired from political office, Chen Yingzhong of the Left Office was composing the *Zunyao Lu* (Record of Honoring Yao) for presentation to the Emperor;
those in power were envious of him and claimed that the Master had significantly assisted in its editing.
In the tenth month of the first year of the Zhenghe era, he was stripped of his monastic robes (*saṃghāṭī*) and banished overseas. In the spring of the third year, he encountered a general amnesty.
He returned to Jiangxi. That winter, he was again arrested and imprisoned in Bingzhou. The following year, he was released and traveled between Jiufeng and Dongshan.

Wearing informal, carefree attire, he amused himself with his literary compositions. Intending to travel from Xi'an to Hengyang and Xiangtan, he was detained by local authorities because he appeared aged;
furthermore, being accused of being a "mad Daoist," they took him to be an associate of Zhang Huaisu and cast him into the Nanchang prison for interrogation.
After more than a hundred days, as it was not yet time for a general amnesty, he returned to the Southern Terrace in Western Xiangxi.

He continued to reside there, naming his dwelling the "Mingbai Hermitage" (The Hermitage of Clarity and Transparency) and composing an inscription for it himself. The preface states: "My karmic ties to this world are deep and heavy; I have long been bound by my past habits.

I am fond of discussing the rise and fall, the right and wrong, and the success and failure of matters from antiquity to the present. Many of my associates mock and rebuke me for this, but Chen Yingzhong alone said:"
It does not obstruct the Way from the very beginning, much like smoke and clouds in mountains and rivers, or the blossoming and flourishing of plants and trees.
What is called "exquisite and charming diligence" is known by my heart to be mere play; yet I do not cease to practice it.

In the spring of the first year of the Daguan era, I thatched a hut at Linchuan and named it "Mingbai" (Clear Understanding), desiring to discipline myself with severity. When Yingzhong heard of this, he...

Severing the vital ford, the paths of both ordinary beings and sages are cut off. At such a time, one perceives no sentient beings to be delivered, nor does one perceive a Buddha-fruit to be clearly realized.
There are no afflictions to be eliminated, and no Bodhi to be attained. Only the fundamental essence is revealed;
its function is majestic and grand, appearing and disappearing, rolling up and unfolding with great sovereign freedom, whether in heaven or hell, or within a tiger’s den.

Throughout the palaces of Māra, there are sites of enlightenment; in every place, there are the deeds of the Buddha. Although this is so, one must nevertheless reach this ground before it can be attained.

This matter does not arise from cultivation or realization, nor does it depend on the mediation of words; it is nothing other than the illumination of wondrous wisdom, transcendent and uniquely liberated.
If you have not yet reached this state, you should forget emotions and sever all discursive thoughts, observing with profound and earnest attention. After a long time, [the truth will manifest].
Spontaneously, the clouds and mists disperse; the solitary moon is white and full. When the sand and pebbles are exhausted, the reality of the whole is finally seen.

It is also said: "The ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. The peach blossoms are red, the plum blossoms are white—who says they are all of one color in their harmonious blend?
The swallows chatter, the orioles sing—who says 'guan-guan' is but a single sound? If you do not penetrate the pivot of the Patriarch, you will remain stuck.
"Son, you are vainly identifying mountains and rivers as your own eyes. He further said: "At the hour of the Rabbit (dawn), when putting it into use, there is no need for clever artifice.
Holding up his staff, he said: "The staff spans the mountains and rivers; the entire great earth is spanned at once. The staff stabilizes the mountains and rivers."
The great earth is suddenly solid; the Dharma preached by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions cannot serve as a metaphor for this.
It is utterly free from error and lacks artifice; it is like applying moxa to a healed scar until it burns.

If one can investigate its source here, only then will one penetrate the Zen monk’s upper orifice. "What is the Zen monk’s upper orifice? He struck the meditation seat and descended from it. Furthermore:
It is said: Formerly, a monk asked Zhaozhou, “What is the meaning of ‘non-transmigration’? Zhaozhou made a gesture with his hand as if flowing water; the monk attained realization.
Again, another monk asked Fayan, “‘Do not grasp at appearances; it is like never having moved from the start.
How does one not grasp at appearances while seeing that which is unmoving? Fayan replied, “The sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night. His...
The assembly also had an awakening. If you can attain clarity here, you will see the Way: "The whirlwind topples the mountains, yet they remain ever still;
the rivers rush in competition toward the sea, yet they do not flow. If this is not yet so, I shall speak further for you: "Heaven revolves to the left; Earth revolves to the right."
From antiquity to the present, how many cycles have passed? The golden crow flies; the jade hare runs. Hardly has it emerged from the gates of the sea when it already sets behind the green mountains.
The waves of the rivers and streams stretch far and wide; the surges of the Huai and Ji flow on endlessly. They enter directly into the vast blue ocean, flowing day and night.
He then raised his voice and said, "Virtuous practitioners of Chan, do you still see that which is like suchness, unmoving? He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended from it.
He spoke again: "The song of the oriole is hoarse at first; the call of the swallow is fresh upon its arrival. Do not be startled by the white of my two鬓 (hair-tufts)."
Once again, spring has arrived. Upon the forest trees, flowers spread like brocade; along the embankments, grasses weave a carpet.

Who would have known that the essence of creation is, fundamentally, the body of the Dharma King? Raising his whisk, he said: "Look! Look! If you can recognize this, the Ocean Seal will radiate light."

If this were not yet the case, worldly afflictions would first arise; [the Master] struck the meditation seat and descended from it. The Master resided at Taiping for eight years, during which his school’s influence shook the world.
In the second year of the Zhenghe era, an imperial edict was issued inviting him to reside at Zhihai in the Eastern Capital.

On the ninth day of the tenth month, he ascended the hall at the Main Gate of the Great Xiangguo Monastery. An imperial envoy was dispatched to deliver incense, and the Junior Director of the Court of State Ceremonial brought the official letter. Furthermore—
The Emperor bestowed gold and jewels to provide for the vegetarian feast. After the Master had expressed his gratitude and offered prayers for the Emperor, a monk asked:

"As soon as you ascended the lion throne, you burned celestial incense; regarding these words of prayer for the Emperor, we request that you speak them quickly. The Master replied: "Auspicious clouds envelop the palace halls; auspicious vapors fill the universe. The monk pressed further:
"A single *dharma-flower* blooms in the capital; its fame shall henceforth spread throughout the human world."
The Master said, “It is a distinct springtime of its own. [The student] said, “The assembly on Vulture Peak remains as if it were still there.
The Master asked, “What was the matter at the assembly on Vulture Peak? [The student] said, “Tomorrow, a wise ruler will surely discern it;

the student bows three times to express gratitude for the Master’s kindness. The Master said, “Let it circulate freely as you wish. A questioner asked, “The ancient melody of Great Peace has long spread its refined resonance. The student [comes] up...”
[The monk] came forward and requested, "I beg the Master to grant me an instruction. The Master said, "There is an inch on the end of the ruler, but no stars on the tail of the scale.

The monk said, "If that is so, then the vast waves of the ocean of wisdom universally bestow their remaining moisture. The Master said, "The true does not conceal the false; the crooked does not hide the straight.

The monk asked, "What is produced upon the ground where there is neither yin nor yang? The Master said, "What do you call 'the ground where there is neither yin nor yang'? The monk said, [further questioning].
"A numinous sprout and auspicious herb are but ordinary matters; the *utpala* flower is spring beyond the mundane world. The Master said, "Thank you for your offerings," and then continued:
"Let us cease this questioning. Have you not heard it said: 'To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the great void'?"
Exhausting the pivotal mechanisms of the world is like casting a single drop into a vast ocean; how much more so is the Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs, the primordial source of all Buddhas.
Within all sentient beings, from the most minute insect to those with consciousness, there is neither increase nor decrease. Only those who are sage among sages can truly know this.

I have reverently heard that the late Emperor Shizheng Renzong composed a poem on Cultivating the Mind which says: "The First Patriarch sat in meditation at Shaolin; he did not transmit scriptures or teachings."

It is simply the transmission of the mind. If those who come after awaken to the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā), they will realize that the profound principle of the Secret Seal has been wondrous from the beginning.
I dare ask you all: what is the nature of True Suchness? What is the wondrous principle of the Secret Seal?

Even if Maudgalyāyana or Śāriputra possessed their wisdom and supernatural powers, upon reaching this point, they would surely have their blades blunted and their tongues tied. Fortunately, today I have encountered such a swift [opportunity].

He then opened the hall for the sake of the nation; having found the Way, he proceeded directly, for what need was there to fear the strange laughter of onlookers? He then raised his whisk and said: "Look, look!
Is this not the true suchness-nature of all of you? Is this not the wondrous principle of the secret seal of all of you?"
If you can see it here, we shall together repay the grace of the state. If this is not yet so, I shall have occasion to discuss it further (here ends the formal expression of thanks).

He continued: "Regarding what was just mentioned—that the First Patriarch sat in meditation at Shaolin, transmitting not the scriptures and teachings but only the Mind—tell me, how is this Mind transmitted?
Our Emperor Renzong reigned for over forty years; during his leisure from the myriad affairs of state..."
Pay close attention to this Way. Once it has been realized within the mind, it is then expressed through speech, circulating endlessly for later generations to follow as a standard.
When our ancestor Bodhidharma first arrived at Shaolin, the Second Patriarch stood in attendance and asked, "My mind is not yet at peace;

I beg the Master to bring it to rest. Bodhidharma said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall bring it to rest for you. The Second Patriarch replied, "I have searched for my mind, but I cannot find it."
"It cannot be attained. Bodhidharma said, "I have finished granting you peace of mind. Thereupon, the Second Patriarch attained sudden and great enlightenment.
From then on, he transmitted the robe and the Dharma, succeeding to the patriarchal position. But tell me, what was it that the Second Patriarch realized at that time?

Those of noble spirit understand at a mere glance; those of superficial influence find it difficult to comprehend in the end. I have composed these humble verses to provide a small aid in their manifestation.
Seeking the mind, nothing is found; thus one rests in peace and attains realization. How can this compare to the depth of non-realization? Ten thousand-foot azure pools reflect the white autumn moon;
a single cry of an old monkey resounds from beyond the clouds. Dust accumulates to form mountains; iron is forged into needles.

Before Mount Shaoshi, there is no divergent path; those who travel to and fro encounter but rugged precipices. The Imperial Censor-in-Chief, Lord Deng Gongzhi Chang, submitted a memorial requesting that he be granted the purple robe.
Master Fojian’s name was [bestowed]; he remained at Zhikai for three years, repeatedly submitting petitions to decline and return to the mountains.

Soon thereafter, he received imperial permission to reside at Jiangshan on Mount Jangning. On the eighth day of the tenth month in the seventh year of the Zhenghe era, he bathed and changed his robes.

Seated upright in his chamber, he wrote several scrolls of letters to his old friends by hand; then, setting down his brush, he passed away. His sacred remains and *śarīra* relics were enshrined in a stupa on this very mountain.
The Master was richly endowed with talent and learning; his grasp of the Way and its principles was profound, and his practice was sublime.

At that time, the monastic communities throughout the land looked up to him in admiration, considering him one who had deeply attained the *samādhi* of the true mechanism and great function of Dongshan. Initially, he received [the transmission from] Tai...

On ordinary days, he would immediately assume the proper ritual demeanor and knock at the chamber of Lingyuan, requesting him to say: "As one who oversees the community while residing in this monastery, what should take precedence?
Lingyuan replied, "There is nothing else; you should simply place your staff, alms bowl, and traveling pack between the pillars in the abbot’s quarters.
To come and go as light as a novice monk—this is sufficient. The Master followed this practice throughout his life, and it subsequently became the standard for the patriarchs of a generation.
Xingyun’s eulogy says:
I have often heard that when Chan Master Cishou first appeared in the world at Zifu Temple in Zhenzhou, he succeeded Chan Master Jingzhao as his Dharma heir.

He soon withdrew from his seat and resided at Mount Jiangshan. There, within the assembly of Fojian, I listened to the topics presented during his night lectures; they were all matters he had long cultivated.
He was not yet enlightened, and his mind remained unsettled by these differences. Suddenly one night, beneath the words of Fojian, he attained great awakening.
He immediately wished to offer incense and change his lineage affiliation to that of Fojian, but Fojian firmly declined him and would not permit it. Alas!

How could there have been anyone in this degenerate age who deceives the world and betrays his official duty, seeking to change his lineage for the sake of a monastery and requesting a fly-whisk with gold? Could such a person ever have been anything other than a slave to Fojian?

Chan Master Longmen Yuan, whose Dharma name was Qingyuan, was born into the Li clan as a native of Linqiong in Shu. He entered the monastic order and received full ordination at the age of fourteen.

He once relied upon a Vinaya master to thoroughly investigate its doctrines. Later, while reading the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he reached the passage: "This Dharma is not to be grasped through thought or discrimination."

He attempted to resolve his doubts by posing these questions to a lecturer, but none could provide an answer. He then remarked, "The study of doctrinal principles and technical terminology is not the means for resolving the great matter of birth and death.
Consequently, he abandoned his former studies and traveled south to the regions of the Yangtze and Huai rivers.

There, he visited various monasteries in succession until he heard that the teacher Yan Dao at Taiping Monastery in Shuzhou was a master of the foremost caliber. He went to seek him out, and as soon as Yan saw him—

The Master was deeply impressed by his extraordinary character, believing him capable of upholding the Dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*). He stood like a cliff, without seeking any assistance, hoping he would reach profound realization.
The Master lived there for seven years, never uttering a single word in vain. One day, while poking at a fire, he suddenly attained awakening and spoke this verse:
"Deeply poking the fire, something has emerged; All the affairs of my life are just like this. From this, he attained thorough penetration and transcendent mastery.

His eloquence was sharp and swift; none dared to meet his鋒 (fēng, "edge" or "onslaught"). Monks vied with one another to seek him out as their teacher, yet he remained increasingly silent and self-effacing, never considering himself to have attained anything.

He lived in seclusion at Dazhong Hermitage on Mount Simian. At that time, the newly established Chongning Temples throughout the empire were selecting individuals to occupy these positions, and Wang Huanzhi, the Governor of Shu, invited the Master to serve as its abbot. Not long after, he withdrew, coinciding with the vacancy at Longmen.
Xī subsequently filled the vacancy. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Those who study the Way have two kinds of illnesses: first, riding a donkey while searching for a donkey;
second, having already mounted the donkey, being unwilling to dismount. Now, to mount the donkey and yet continue to search for one is truly a grievous illness.
Longmen says: 'Do not seek. A person of keen intelligence recognizes this immediately and discards the act of seeking."
His illness struck; his frantic mind was finally stilled. Once he had recognized the donkey, however, he mounted it and refused to dismount.
This particular ailment is the most difficult to cure. Longmen said to him: "Do not mount it! You yourself are the donkey. The entire great earth is this very donkey. But how can you mount it?
If you mount it, you may be certain your illness will not depart. If you do not mount it, the ten directions of the world are vast and empty."
When these two ailments depart simultaneously, the mind becomes tranquil and free from affairs; this is what is called being a man of the Way.
This is why Zhaozhou asked Nanquan, "What is the Way? Nanquan replied, "The ordinary mind is the Way. From that moment on, Zhaozhou suddenly ceased his frantic pursuit.

Having recognized the sickness of the patriarchs and the sickness of the Buddhas, there was nothing he could not penetrate. Later, as he traveled everywhere throughout the various regions, none surpassed him.
This was because he had recognized their sickness. He also said: "Where is the Old Śākyamuni? He himself replied, "What?
Then he asked again, "Where is Master Bodhidharma? He himself replied, "He is right here; what do you say?"
This fundamental principle is not at all easy to clarify. If you can understand it here and now, only then will you know that the True Dharma is eternally abiding.
Most Zen practitioners simply say that the very moment the koan is raised is it. But what about when your body breaks up and your life ends?
Or when you are so ill that you cannot speak? You must realize and enter into it for yourself; have you not seen the monk?
He asked Deshan, "Where have all the sages of the past gone? Deshan said, "What? What? [The student] thought, "Is it that 'what? itself is the sages?
If you all do not understand through words, you will fall into the flow of their sounds and echoes.
Even if you do not fall into sounds and phrases, you will still fall into their state of wordlessness and silence. This—
In reality, there is nothing. Your understanding is merely a matter of intellectual speculation. If you harbor even a single thread of thought, you have already strayed from the essential point.
Even if you were to apply the profound mysteries and wondrous meanings to it, they would certainly not fit. Yet, it is also not possible to remain entirely without reflection.
You must personally realize it yourself; you must see it clearly and without doubt. Furthermore, he said: "There is a certain kind of school..."
The Master says to people: "Do not engage in calculating or reasoning; as soon as you open your mouth, there is no connection, and it does not correspond with him.
You must recognize it prior to the empty kalpa, where there is no speech at all. Furthermore, there is another kind of master who says to people:
"You foolish fellows! Why do you not understand this one segment? First, take your own mind and make it into a conceptual trap."
Then you take that mind to seek realization; this is called "nailing down the stake. You run around the stake just like that, and so it is transmitted;
you accept it just like that. You beat the meditation seat and brandish the whisk to employ it, calling this "using the mind with the mind.
It is just like sitting on a balloon; what peace and ease is there in it? It is also like a frog puffing out its breath.
"Your understanding is like this; it is as if a thick black mist were shrouding everything before you.
The Master resided at Longmen for twelve years, and his reputation for the Way spread far and wide. Scholars from all quarters would say, "I must take Longmen as my teacher."
Consequently, they gathered beneath his seat until there was no room to accommodate them. The Master responded to their inquiries with ease, never showing even a trace of weariness.
He presented several pieces of intricate instruction, which the students collected and compiled, titling it *The Essentials of the Mind* (*Xinyao*).
Its summary states: "One should not establish boundaries within the boundless. If one establishes boundaries, then that very boundless emptiness will follow after you. Therefore...
One who understands emptiness has no conceptualization of emptiness. If a person attempts to name or characterize the mind through words, they will ultimately not find the mind.

If they do not attempt to name or characterize the mind through words, they likewise do not find the mind. This is because words are originally used to name and characterize the mind; thus, they cannot be found.
It is also because the absence of words is originally the mind’s lack of being named or characterized; thus, it cannot be found. All such various realizations are necessarily so.

"It does not accord with one's own mind. The Patriarch said, "It is simply a matter of silent resonance (*moqi*). He further said, "As for how the Way is realized, it is merely a matter of being without deluded thoughts (*wangnian*).
If a person recognizes these as deluded thoughts and intentionally exerts effort to stop them, it is because they perceive the existence of deluded thoughts.
Because they perceive the existence of deluded thoughts, they intentionally apply contemplative observation; yet even this correct principle is seen as having deluded thoughts."
Furthermore, knowing that delusion is fundamentally the Way means there is no delusion at all; therefore, one who has attained the Way has nothing to acquire.
It is also said: "Realization means the cessation of subject and object. This does not mean there is some separate, mysterious principle apart from the ordinary course of daily life.

For instance, when seeing forms, that is the moment of realization; when hearing sounds, that is the moment of realization; when drinking water or eating gruel, that is the moment of realization—one by one.

To sever the subject and object is not something achieved through long-term practice or the application of refinement; it is a matter already present before one’s eyes. Yet worldly people do not recognize it, which is termed "wandering in saṃsāra.
Thus it is said: "Only through realization can it be known; it is difficult to fathom. It is also said: "Those who study the Way clearly know that such a thing exists.
Why then do they fail to grasp its essential meaning and remain in perpetual doubt? This is because their faith has not reached its ultimate limit and their doubt has not yet become profound. Only...

The profound and the ultimate, faith and doubt—these are truly matters of fact. Failing to reflect back upon them in this manner, one becomes confused and bewildered, unable to discern their origins, and comes to a halt midway.
To be able to turn back and examine oneself—there is no second person who can do so. Since these are called "matters," how could they be known otherwise?
If one knows that [other thoughts] are deluded reflections, then these matters will not be lost. Furthermore, it is said: "The Way does not..."

It is only after speaking and pointing that [the truth] is revealed; for its essence is inherently ever-present. Speaking and pointing are merely the functional applications of the path of skillful means.

Even the moment of awakening is but a temporary crossroads. Whether one attains realization through speech, enters by means of pointing, or knows the way home through spontaneous self-awakening, in the end there is no difference in the matter.
One simply reaches the source of the ultimate mind and comes to rest. It is further said:
People say that one must first attain awakening before practicing this; this belongs to the gate of remedial means (*pratipakṣa*).
Although even the Chan school permits treating [delusions] with right knowledge and vision, for the person in question, it is not necessary to be like this. Furthermore, it is said:

"When people do not recognize the question, they answer according to what has been asked, not realizing that they are actually asking themselves. To whom would they wish to give an answer? When people do not recognize the answer, they consequently...
To speak of "arising views" is merely to answer oneself out of ignorance; what purpose or meaning could there be in that? Therefore it is said:

"It is all for you to look upon, to look upon. It is also said: "From of old, there have been two kinds of skillful means (*upāya*): there are the skillful means of reality, which refers to the uninterrupted teaching of non-existence;
and there are the skillful means of expediency, which refers to the wondrous responding to the various capacities of sentient beings. If one follows the skillful means of reality..."

It is simply a matter of being able to enter without relying on deliberation; the nature itself is divinely enlightened. Seeking it, one finds no regression; its wondrous function is as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
If one enters through skillful means (*upāya*), one may sit and don the robes, but one must look back for oneself before it is truly attained.
This should not yet be taken as the ultimate. These two kinds of skillful means are both a single Dharma; one must not lose them for even a moment. Study!

Reflect upon this. It is further said: To awaken the mind and see one's nature, one should be like Xuefeng and Xuansha; to tread the path and practice the truth, one should be like Nanquan and Zhaozhou.
Those who study nowadays merely take the skillful means of the ancients to be the Way of Chan, failing to realize that they must participate in the same realization as those ancients.
If, throughout the twelve periods of the day, one studies the Way without abandoning it for even a single moment, such a person—though...

One has not yet attained entry. Every thought-moment is already cultivation. What is commonly called "cultivation" does not go beyond the Chan gate of purifying the three karmas and six sense faculties;
there is no need for it to be otherwise. Why? Because within the gate of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), every thought-moment is equal to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Thus, in all circumstances, there is naturally no fault or affliction. After a long time, the mind-ground becomes penetratingly clear.

In former times, people were able to attain fulfillment in all respects; this was called the Samādhi of One Practice. People of the present age possess no meditative power at all and have not opened their eye of wisdom;

consequently, their words and phrases regarding spiritual conditions and circumstances result only in contentious debate. Such mental activity of arising and ceasing is the case. Now, the study of Chan is no small matter.
Yet, if one has not yet used it to transcend Buddhas and Patriarchs, it will not be difficult to do so once one seeks that essential transcendence. Indeed.

Huimeng’s reputation for his practice spread to the imperial court, and by imperial decree, he was transferred to Baoshan in Hezhou. After more than a year, he declined the post on account of illness.
At that time, Chan Master Yuanwu was residing at Jiangshan; as they had long been close friends and spiritual companions, Huimeng went there to rely upon him.

He once composed the "Three Self-Examinations," which were held in high esteem throughout the monastic community. Furthermore, he observed that those who engage in the "question-and-answer" (wenda) method of recent times do not know how to properly extend [the inquiry].
Regarding the meaning of posing questions and seeking instruction, later generations have handed down a tradition of using mostly words of praise and benediction.

Whether these are addressed to officials present or offered as solemn arrangements by lay donors (dānapati), they all lack the true spirit of a monk (*śramaṇa*). The Master detested this deeply and cautioned them, saying:
"Now, as for engaging in dialogue (*wenhua*), it is to stimulate and exalt the ultimate mystery; it does not lie in proffering many words. Two or three turns are sufficient. What is valued is..."
He gained the trust of the people and did not fall into dissipation to become an object of ridicule for worldly folk.
He also remarked, "The venerable elders of various regions invariably leave behind verses when facing death. How can one bid farewell to the world? For now, let us simply rest in peace.

On the first day before the winter solstice in the second year of the Xuanhua era, having finished his meal, he adjusted his robes, sat in the lotus posture, joined his palms, and passed away with a serene expression. He was fifty-four years of age.
He sat in meditation for forty summers. His disciples enshrined his remains and *śarīra* relics, interring them at the Lingguang Pagoda on Mount Longmen.

The Master’s demeanor was exceptionally refined and extraordinary; his integrity was strict and upright. By nature he was simple and spoke little; even his smiles and movements followed a disciplined measure.

Students, beholding his appearance and deportment, took him to heart as their model. His teaching was broad, expansive, and penetrating, providing a direct and incisive remedy for the meditative ailments of the monastics.

As for his mind, when he reached the point of entering the chamber and grasping the essential framework, all paths were cut off and he transcended words and letters; yet he did not linger in empty, desolate, or frivolous discourse.
Among his disciples, he would not recklessly grant approval unless they had attained a profound realization and verification. In his daily life, he took the Way as his own responsibility.
He did not involve himself in worldly affairs. He once said, "An elder sits upright in his chamber, merely transmitting the Way.

When he associated with scholars and officials, he would not bend to personal gain. If their way accorded with his own, he would joyfully visit them; otherwise, even if they passed his door, he might not grant them an audience.
The gentleman [Fan Zongyan] held him in high esteem. The State Councillor Deng Xunwu memorialized the throne to bestow upon Fiyuan the ceremonial robes of an official.

Regarding his title: when Left Minister Chen Gongguan saw the Master’s recorded sayings (*fayu*), he sighed in admiration, saying, "The heart-essence of all Buddhas and the ocean of the nature of sentient beings—Master Yuanyuan has immersed himself in these depths profoundly.
He was a close friend of Chan Master Lingyuan from their youth, and their inclinations and spiritual practices were largely similar.
His *Guangyu* (Extensive Sayings) from three assemblies, along with his verses and hymns, total tens of thousands of words and circulate in the world.
The commentary states: Yuanwu and Foyan emerged from the same gate of Dongshan; both were tenth-generation descendants of Linji.
While Yuanwu’s fame had already covered the world, Foyan was profound, refined, and pure, fully upholding the orthodox transmission. He was nearly a peer to Yuanwu, racing alongside him.
Students have doubted whether his approach was merely a temporary variation from Yuanwu’s, or as some say, that he was the "Dragon Gate."
"I once lived with Lingyuan, and it was through gradual habituation that this came to be. Alas! How shallow such words are!

I have indeed read the *Longmen lu* three times over, observing how he pointed out the Dharma of the mind; his eloquence was like that of Baizhang and Huangbo, while his poetic verses were like those of Fenyang and Xuedou.
His realization was transcendent, not inferior to the profound subtlety of Xuefeng, and his practice was thorough."
The evidence is clear: he was as upright as Nanquan and Zhaozhou, truly a great master of this age.
How could those who take mere words as Chan and deceive the world ever be fit to recognize one who is in perfect accord with Lingyuan of Longmen?
To summarize the reason why they did not become equals to Yuanwu: it is like the writings of Han Yu and Liu Zongyuan.

Although there are many in the world who delight in Han Yu’s work, unless one is a person of profound insight and broad erudition such as Liu Zongyuan, one cannot fathom the depths of his inner mysteries.
This is why, throughout ten thousand generations, no one has been able to rival him and stand shoulder-to-shoulder with him as a peer. Viewed from this perspective, the two—[Yuanwu and Yuanjue]—...
The legacy of the Master may indeed be seen here.
Chan Master Fāng of Heshan, whose name was Huìfāng and whose dharma title was Chāozōng, was the son of the Gōng family of Línjiāng. He left the household life at Chánjū Temple at the age of...

At nineteen, he passed the scriptural examinations and received ordination. He traveled extensively to consult various spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*). Later, he entered Huanglong and met Chan Master Sīxīn;
their karmic conditions were in accord, and he remained there to serve him. For fourteen years, he stayed by his side.

At that time, Sīxīn held all quarters in high regard, employing a "wall-like" and perilously steep approach as his skillful means (*upāya*); no students could draw near to him, and few were able to enter his circle.
As for Ji: among the vast assembly, he alone proclaimed that the Master was capable of continuing the authentic lineage and entrusted to him the final great matter.
Having received this prophetic mandate, the Master remained in seclusion within the monasteries, yet his reputation grew ever higher.

During the Xuanhong era, he emerged into the world at Longqing in Luochuan and subsequently moved to Heshan, where his school’s influence shook the land. A monk asked: "What is the single seal that seals the void?"
The Master replied, "I imagine you have groped about but failed to find it. [The student] asked, "What is the one seal that seals water?

The Master said, "It is profoundly still. [The student] asked, "What is the one seal that seals mud? The Master said, "The preceding and succeeding correspond. [The student] asked, "What is life within death?
The Master replied, "There is function within illumination. [The student] asked, "What is death within life? The Master replied, "Within function there is..."

Zhao asked, "What is 'constantly dying within death'? The Master replied, "The function of illumination is applied according to the occasion. Zhao asked, "What is 'constantly living within life'? The Master said, "A straightforward exit.
On the anniversary of the passing of Master Sijian (Sixin), a monk asked, "Master Sijian often raised the meaning of the single sandal returning to the West;
what was his intent? The Master said, "Do you see it yet? The monk stepped forward and said, "This very seeing and hearing is not seeing."
