Chan Master Yuanwu Qin, whose dharma name was Keqin and courtesy name Wuzhuo, was the son of the Luo family of Chongning in Pengzhou.

He received the tonsure under Zizheng of Miaoji Monastery and was ordained with the full precepts. He traveled to Chengdu, where he studied the sutras and śāstras under the Great Master Yuanming Minxing.
Peering into its depths, he felt it was insufficient and specifically went to visit Chan Master Sheng of Zhaojue to inquire about the Dharma of the mind.

After a long time, he visited Chan Master Zhenru Zhe at Faguan, where he attained considerable realization. At that time, the Abbot Qing was highly regarded by the assembly as one who had thoroughly studied the Way;

he was especially skilled in the fundamental tenets of the Dongshan (Dongxia) school. The Master associated with him and frequently exhausted the essential points of his teaching. He also once visited Donglin Zhaojue. Shortly thereafter—
He said to Qing: "Donglin is merely a place of conventional reality. Go see the one who propagates the Way at Taiping.
The Master relied on his bold eloquence and sought to contend with him point for point. Taiping was displeased and said, "Can this be used to confront birth and death?

When the solitary lamp shines alone in the Nirvana Hall on another day, you shall test it for yourself. The Master departed because their views did not accord, traveling to Dinghui in Suzhou, where he fell ill.

He nearly died. Reflecting on what he had previously studied, he found that none of it had borne fruit; only Master Yan had not deceived him. Upon recovering from his illness, he immediately packed his bags and returned.
Master Yan rejoiced at his second coming and accepted him as an attendant. It happened that the Transport Commissioner, Lord Chen, entered the mountain to inquire about the Dharma.
As Yan recited a minor erotic poem, he said: "Frequently calling for 'Little Jade' was originally for no reason; I simply wanted the donor..."

Lang recognized the voice. While serving at the Master’s side, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He immediately informed Yan, who said to him, "Today you have truly lost the opportunity before your eyes.
The Master replied, "Today I have truly lost the opportunity before my eyes. Yan said joyfully, "Our school has you; from now on, I can rest easy.
The Master then spoke of this matter to Fojian Qin. Qin did not believe it, so the Master said, "In the past, it was said that Goryeo beats iron."
Mars struck my finger. At first I thought it was a figurative expression; now it has indeed come true. Daoyin was startled and speechless.
At that time, Chan Master Fuyan was still young, yet the Master would always guide him on every matter. Later, both masters attained great enlightenment.
Consequently, the two from the Yan lineage—Daoyin and Daoyuan—became renowned for their excellence, such that they were called the "Three Heroes" of the monastic community. Yan...
When the Fifth Patriarch was transferred [to another temple], the Master took charge of the monastery’s affairs and was just beginning construction on the eastern kitchen.

In the courtyard stood a fine tree; Yanyou said, "Even if this tree obstructs us, it must not be cut down. The Master nevertheless cut it down. Yanyou brandished his staff and pursued the Master, who fled to avoid him.
Suddenly, he had a profound realization, saying, "This is precisely Linji's way! He then seized the staff and said, "Old thief! I know you well! Yanyou—
He laughed heartily and departed. From that time on, he was assigned a seat to preach the Dharma. At the beginning of the Chongning era, he returned to Shu because his mother was elderly.
He later took charge of the Shaojue Monastery, but after some time, he resigned. In Jingzhou, he met with the Chancellor Zhang Wujin and discussed the essential subtleties of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Zhang’s phrasing was elegant and refined, and his profound understanding of the ultimate meaning was thorough and penetrating; unconsciously, Zhang moved forward to sit closer on the mat. The Master said, "This is the true realm."
"How does this compare with the essential purport of the Chan school? Wujin asked. The Master said, "It is certainly not different.
Wujin replied, "What connection is there? The Master spoke slowly, "The ancients said: 'Not seeing form is but half the teaching; one must further know the time for the full presentation.
Only when you have penetrated through to the core will you see the workings of Deshan and Linji. At these words, Wujin was suddenly enlightened.
[The Master] said: "I have long harbored doubts regarding Xuedou’s phrase 'the great furnace and the refined gold. Only now do I realize that there is no place for him to be grasped.
The Teacher said: "Some time ago, I had a verse which said: 'A thunderclap resounds directly from the crown of the head; the needle extracts the fatal illness of the incurable.'"
By chance, his views coincided with those of the Chancellor. Wujin said with joy, "I have always feared that the Way of our ancestors was gradually declining;
now, we may truly say we have met a 'Daoist robe-clad Guan Yiwu. The Prefect of Lizhou invited him to reside at Jia Shan. Not long after, he moved to Daolin in Xiangxi.
Initially, Master Tan had been recommended by Zhou Gong, and Liu Zhixu wished to see the Master. Upon this occasion, [the Prefect] judged him by his external appearance.

He did not treat him with much ceremony; however, upon seeing him preside over the hall and deliver his formal discourse (*kai-tang ti-chang*), which was wondrous beyond the reach of thought, he began to increase his respect.
At the end of the Zhenghe era, by imperial decree, he was transferred to Mount Jiangshan in Jinling, where the Way of the Dharma flourished greatly.
A monk asked, "What is the ground of ultimate reality (*shiji lidi*)? He replied, "Why do you not realize it before you have even asked? The monk said, "How can one realize it before one has asked?"
The Master said, "I have been following you all along. Xuefeng advanced and said, "A favorable opportunity is hard to encounter; may I ask one more question?
The Master said, "Forgetting what came before and losing track of what follows. Xuefeng said, "If we discuss this matter, it is like the spark struck from flint.

But as for the time before we met, how was it then? The Master said, "Even three thousand miles away, one still encounters him. Xuefeng said, "In that case, I have met the Master outside of sound and form. The Master replied, "Yes."
[The student] said, "He has even pierced through his nostrils. [The student] asked, "A loyal minister does not fear death, and thus is able to establish the great name of the world;
a brave warrior does not regard his life, and thus is able to accomplish the great deeds of the world. I wonder, how about those in the family of the patch-robed monks?
The Master said, "To have one's majesty shake the entire realm is not considered extraordinary. [The student] said, "If that is so, then they sit and cut off the ten directions like a wall."

[Zhang] stood at a height of a thousand *ren*. The Master said, "Look at the arrow! [Zhang] asked, "Regarding 'not falling into cause and effect' and 'not being oblivious to cause and effect,' are they the same or different?
The Master said, "Two adamantine rings. [Zhang] said, "When Guishan shook the door panel three times, what was that?
The Master said, "Those who do not share the same path will not raise this up. [Zhang] said, "In that case, it is like beating the drum and playing the lute."
The two met at the master’s residence. The Master said, "Is your name not quite grand? The monk replied, "One must not suppress the noble to make them base.
The Master said, "Bring me a phrase from the realm of reality. The monk said, "Since I became a servant to Mr. Pan, I have also come to know how to remain unashamed before others.
The Master said, "Quickly prostrate three times. The monk said, "In the past, someone asked Touzi, 'What is...'"
The Ten-Bodied Tamer [the Buddha] descended from his meditation seat and stood there. What was his intent? The Master said, "Cast from solid iron.
The monk asked, "Why did he say, 'While greedily gazing at the white waves, one loses the hand-oar'? The Master said, "Go away and take this upon yourself.

A monk asked, "Regarding the saying, 'Does the head meet with the light, or does the head meet with the dark? why did the Ancient Virtuous One immediately return to his quarters? The Master picked up [a staff].
[The Master] held up his staff. The student stepped forward and said, "I am about to let it loose; how would you, Reverend, counter it? The Master said, "This wild fox spirit!
[The student] asked, "When the Field for Selecting Buddhas opens, those of superior capacity realize the full proof. How do you instruct one who is not deluded regarding the immediate occasion?"
The Master said, "One leap directly into the ground of the Tathāgata. [The student] asked, "Without obscuring the person of original nature, I ask the Master to cast his eyes upward.
Why did the Great Master Mazu look straight down? The Master said, "There is an eye upon the crown of the head.
[The student] asked, "As for this single stringless lute, only you, Master, can play it wondrously. Why did the Great Master Mazu look straight up? The Master said, "In the darkness..."
[He] was able to extract the bones [of the teaching]. [Xuefeng] said, "I do not know for certain: is it that which looks directly upward, or is it that which looks directly downward?
The Master said, "Do not slander Great Master Ma. [Xuefeng] said, "But how can one deny that 'When the dragon’s sleeve is swept aside, the whole body is revealed;

where the Elephant King walks, there are no traces of foxes'? The Master said, "Fortunately, Layman Pang has provided the testimony. [Xuefeng] asked, "If one knows the 'eye within the phrase,' what is above it?"
When someone comes forward to challenge him from above, he directly applies the full decree of Mahākāla. He prays that you will grant expedient means to receive all capacities.
The Master said, "It is not as good as one who knows nothing at all. [The student] asked, "If there is no iron hammer with a hole in it, what use is there? The Master said:
"Indeed, it goes thus," [the student] said. "Though this is the fundamental matter, it is not yet the upward-reaching mechanism. The Master said, "Scattering sparks, the solitary light flashes forth.
[The student] said, "But what of the arrow behind the head? The Master cannot save you from that. The Master said, "That is merely dragging through mud and water.
He once addressed the assembly, saying: "In such a way, in such a way—both are illuminated. Not in such a way, not in such a way—neither are they illuminated."
How dark! Yet within this "not-so," there is "so"; the light is hidden within the dark. Within this "so," there is "not-so"; the dark is hidden within the light.
Suppose, for a moment, that even the very seat is removed—this dismantling of all established structures is, in every respect, a matter of striking the hand and wounding the blade.
Tell me, what would you call this? Reaching this point, it is high with nothing above and deep with no bottom; it exhausts all horizons.
Within the limits of empty space, down to the most minute particle of dust, it is pure, naked, and brilliantly clear—this is the bottomless almsbowl and the shadowless staff.
Before Mount Xiong’er, beneath the peaks of Shaolin, the Old Barbarian sat for nine years in a state of chilling stillness.
Guarding these idle furnishings amidst deep snow, one must reach the point where emotions are forgotten and intentions cast aside, where principles are exhausted and views grow still;
only then is there one who can truly take it up. But tell me: when both light and dark are simultaneous, when both letting go and gathering are simultaneous—is this establishing or is it ordinary?
Even if it is neither of these, it is still not the ultimate point. So, what is the ultimate point? *Bai* (Split!).

The Flower Peak opens up, reaching to the heavens; the Yellow River is released, flowing with surging currents. During the Xuande era of the Xuanhe period, he was summoned by imperial decree to reside at Tianning Monastery in the Eastern Capital.

When the Sovereign (the future Emperor Gaozong) was still the Prince of Kang, he repeatedly requested that [the Master] propagate the teachings. There is a verse which says: "Most simple and most easy, most supreme and most noble;
it passes over the crown of the thousand sages, inconceivable within and beyond the world. At that time, however, [the Emperor] held him in high esteem...
While the Crown Prince resided in the Eastern Palace, the Master spoke before the Emperor (Taishang) regarding a prophecy concerning his future supreme status.

In the first year of the Jianyan era, Li Boji, the Chancellor of Ning Province, submitted a memorial requesting that he reside at Jinshan. When the imperial carriage visited Wuyang, an edict was issued summoning him for an audience.

The Emperor questioned him on the essential teachings of the Western Regions (Indic Buddhism), to which he replied: "Your Majesty governs the world through the principle of filial piety; the Dharma of the Western Regions unifies all things through the single mind."

Although the ultimate and the conventional differ, within the single mind there is never any interval between them. The Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Yuangwu.
He requested to retire to Yunju Mountain to spend his final years; the court provided generous provisions for his journey. The following year after he arrived at Yunju, he returned to Sichuan.
The Grand Master Wang Boshao welcomed him to reside at Zhaojue. On the fifth day of the eighth month in the fifth year of the Xiangxing era, he passed away.

He manifested illness and was about to pass away. His attendant held a brush and requested a verse for him. He wrote: "I have already attained the state beyond effort; there is no need to leave behind a verse. I have merely responded to conditions as they arose.
Take care, take care! Having cast aside the brush, he passed away. He was seventy-three years of age and had spent fifty-five summer retreats in seated meditation.

He was posthumously titled Chan Master Zhijue, and his stupa was named Jizhao (Tranquil Illumination). Initially, the Imperial Secretary Deng Zichang submitted a memorial requesting that he be granted [this title].

He was granted the title of Master of the Buddha-Fruit (Fuguo) and the honorific robe. Wherever he went, scholars and gentlemen would visit him to inquire about the Way, never failing for even a single day.

The Master’s gate of enlightenment was vast, and his exposition of the Dharma was eloquent and profound; whether proceeding forward or retreating, he was unimpeded, such that everyone was awed and submissive, deeming him a peerless being they had never encountered before.

Even when receiving guests until the late hours of the night, once the guests had departed, he would invariably take up a torch and open his scrolls to study the principles of the religious teachings.
Shu read everything there was to read. When he was first in Jinling, the Grand Master Wang Yanzhao once asked for instruction regarding Xuedou’s statement:
"Of these three men who are 'men of no affairs,' which one is superior? Shu said, "Right now, they must all receive a beating. The Commander did not understand the meaning;
Shu questioned him further. The Commander struck his knee with his hand. At that time, the monks were gathered in a circle around them, and Shu pointed to them and said: [The text ends here.]
"This group has inverted their understanding; how could they ever penetrate the insights of the ancients? Shuai departed in displeasure.
He subsequently sent a poem for the master to have engraved on stone, but the master concealed it. On another day, Yanzhao entered the mountain and asked where the poem was located.
The Master said, "In ancient times, gifts were bestowed to manifest virtue; now, the Great Master merely offers me satire.
How could I dare to consider what is inappropriate as appropriate? The Commander (Shuai) then bowed, his stern expression cleared, and departed.

Subsequently, Ji Shanzhen, who was acting as the Acting Governor of Yuanzhou, entered the mountain and composed a poem containing the line "the sea of chrysanthemum. However, according to the *Donghan zhi* (Annals of the Eastern Han),...

There was a man named Pu Changhai. When the Master (Daoyuan) approached him to verify certain points, Pu realized he had been mistaken. Someone advised him, saying, "You should not contend with the Master over poetry;
you fear it might bring about disaster. The Master laughed and said, "How could I have done this out of necessity? Previously, I rejected the poems of the Prince;

now, although the new Governor’s verses are fine, I did not dare to have them carved [on stone]. Therefore, I exposed his error, simply because I did not wish to let the principal subject be inscribed upon the stone."
His decisiveness in the face of critical moments was such as this. His nature was gentle and easygoing, and he did not concern himself with worldly affairs.

In his later years, his realization of the Way grew ever more profound, yet his refined character remained unchanged. When some suggested that he should assume a more imposing and dignified bearing, the Master said:

"Our Buddha gathers beings through compassion and regards all equally. I always act with such sincerity, yet I still fear falling short; how much less would I dare alter my mind by shifting between manifesting and concealing myself, or by being harsh?"
"He presided over the community with such detachment; how could this be the conduct of a mere śramaṇa? His noble character was vast and expansive, always yielding to others.
Thus, for nearly forty years while he presided over the world and governed the Dharma, there was never a single person who violated his rules and regulations."
The Eulogy says: Our Patriarch’s legacy from of old was to penetrate the fundamental source through wondrous awakening.

Yet, as the world presses on toward decline and heterodox paths flourish daily, none but those who are like dragons coiled or phoenixes soaring—those who plumb the depths and investigate the subtle—can avoid turning their reins back at the City of Transformation.
Yuanwu was truly one such; his virtue and Way were complete, his learning insatiable, and his fame and station exalted.
Yet his resolve became increasingly humble; he was truly a model for his generation.
Initially, among the scholars of the two lineages of Huanglong and Yangqi, there were many who harbored private biases, competing for superiority and showing no mutual respect.

Thereupon, the Great Being Lingyuan composed the "Stele for Master Wuzu Yan’s Correct Continuation," thereby promoting him as the "Correct Continuation. Later, Yuanwu was further able to strictly uphold his own school.
In his private quarters, when he faced the Emperor, he blended the ultimate truth and the mundane world within a single mind;

when he associated with scholars and officials, he exhausted himself in sincere devotion, enabling them to gain a taste of the Way of the Patriarchs and enter its current, so that every person attained mastery over their own mind.
This is how he brought such great renown upon himself throughout the world. How magnificent!
Chan Master Baofeng Xiang’s name was Jingxiang.
He was the son of the Fu family of Nanfeng, Jianchang. His father, Yi, served as the Magistrate of Yongfeng in Xinzhou until his death.

His mother was surnamed Shangguan. She dreamed that she entered the royal palace during the height of summer and received a pitcher of gruel to drink; it was like nectar. Thereafter, she became pregnant.

Furthermore, his father had a dream in which a crimson banner and a black standard escorted a magnificent man to their home, who declared himself the General of the Northern Frontier (Sai-shang Jiangjun).

The next day, [the child] was born; the Master therefore named him Sai-shang Gong. From his youth, he was alert and quick-witted, with a passion for learning and a dedication to memorization and broad reading, such that there was no book he did not examine.
When Lord Yongfeng passed away, his grief was boundless; he felt that nothing short of the supramundane Dharma could suffice to console him.
Having no way to repay [his teacher's kindness], he resolved to leave the household life. At that time, there was a śramaṇa named Qi who was preaching the Dharma at Lingjiu Mountain;

he went to listen and experienced a sudden awakening. He subsequently followed him to shave his head and receive full ordination. He traveled extensively to visit various spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*). Finally, he met Chan Master Daomiao Zhe of Dayun Temple.
Their karmic conditions and resources were in perfect accord, so he attended upon him as a personal attendant. Following him, they entered the capital. After Master Zhe passed away, he carried his...
His remains were returned for burial at Mount Gui. One night, he dreamed of a foreign monk over ten feet tall who bestowed upon him the *Dharmapada*. Its meaning was profoundly subtle and wondrous;

having received it, the Master investigated and savoring its flavor, his realization of the mind-dharma became increasingly clear. He returned to Linchuan and obtained several rooms in an old house beyond the reach of human habitation.
There he secluded himself, refusing to interact with worldly affairs for ten years. During the Daguan era, his fellow practitioner Zizun resided at Donglin.
He treated him with great courtesy and invited him to take the seat of honor. He shared his own mat and robes with him. Before long, the seat at Letan became vacant.

Zhang Sicheng, the Governor of Nanchang, having long heard of the Master’s lofty character, earnestly requested his presence. Although messengers went back and forth four times, the Master remained firmly reclined and did not respond.

Consequently, he entrusted the matter to the Governor of Jiujiang to dispatch him; only then did the Master finally accept the summons. Previously, Dayue had instructed the Master that when his years...
"At fifty, one may become a teacher to others. Now I am fifty-four years old. When he resided at Letan, his school of thought flourished greatly;
there were always five thousand monks under his guidance. His regulations were strict and clear, and the ceremonial etiquette was harmonious and orderly.

From all quarters, people unanimously esteemed and revered him, receiving his teachings as the very ornament of the monastic community. He addressed the assembly, saying: "In general, those who act as spiritual friends..."
To respond appropriately to the capacities of beings and benefit them, one must possess the ten wisdoms that accord with reality (*daśajñāna-satya-samānugata*).

If one does not possess these ten wisdoms that accord with reality, then one cannot distinguish between the monastic and the lay, nor differentiate between the heterodox and the orthodox; such a person is unfit to serve as a guide for gods and humans, and is unable to resolve matters of right and wrong.
It is like a single-wheeled cart or a bird with only one wing: it cannot fly high or travel far. What are the ten ways in which wisdom accords with reality?
First, accord in substance; second, accord in the great task; third, accord in collective practice; fourth, accord in true wisdom; fifth, accord in universal pervasiveness.

Sixth, they are identical in right and wrong; seventh, identical in gain and loss; eighth, identical in life and death; ninth, identical in their roaring voices; tenth, identical in their attainment of entry.
O elders of the various dhyānas, the words and phrases of the patriarchs pervade the ten directions, and the karmic conditions of the old monks throughout the world are many.
Which single phrase among them is "identical in substance" or "identical in the great matter"? Wherein lies their identity in life and death? And so on, up to their identity in...
Only upon being able to enter this state and discern it with clarity does one truly possess the credentials of a patch-robed monk—one who is not of the vulgar crowd.
If you, Master, have not yet clarified or discerned this, and you examine the "eyes" of various quarters [of the Chan school], you will find they do not recognize the source of the student's illness.

If the source of the illness is not recognized, the root of doubt will not be severed. If the root of doubt is not severed, this is called the very foundation of birth and death. Put down your bundle.

When one does not cling to any point and avoids being bitten by the dogs and pigs of conceptual thought, one immediately takes ordinary understanding and hurls it over one's own head, striking it down at the feet.
One says that even if the Buddhas and Patriarchs were to appear, there would be nothing superior to this. Long-time practitioners and high-minded gentlemen may join together to bear witness to this.

But for those who have recently begun their training, there is no need to wait for years or decades; rather, they should look back upon themselves and find that there is absolutely nothing to be approved of. Then—
It was too late for regret. The Master resided at Letan for nearly ten years, until his reputation for the Way reached the capital.
During the Xuanhe era, an imperial decree was issued to transfer him to Mount Jangshan in Jinling; shortly thereafter, he was moved to Yuantong in Jiuyang.

After more than a year, the Governor of Jiangxi sought to take control of Huangbo for himself. The Master learned of this and fled into the mountains of Tong’an, where the traces of both monasteries eventually reached him.

They vied with one another to welcome and invite him, yet in the end, Huangbo obtained him. At the end of the Jianyan era, he retired to Leshan and built a hermitage on Mount Xiufeng, taking that as his title.
He planned to spend the remainder of his life there, but coinciding with the period when the Jin army crossed the southward, he sought refuge in Tiantai.
In the second year of the Shaoxing era, at the request of the Military Governor of Min, he traveled to Mount Daji; however, before he had even crossed the border, he was entreated by Chancellor Fan.

He remained there and submitted a memorial requesting to reside at Hongfu Monastery. Previously, Chan Master Ga’ān had received the command for Hongfu, but passed away before he could enter the monastery.
The Master had long been on intimate terms with Ga’ān; by the time he succeeded him in residing at Fushan, less than a month had elapsed since Ga’ān’s passing.

He then manifested illness and presented his ancient *nāṃsa* (patched robe) along with a letter, entrusting them to his dharma heir, Desheng. On the seventh day of the tenth month, he sat in the lotus posture, addressed the assembly, and passed away.
He was seventy-one years of age and fifty-two years since his ordination (*varṣa*). His body was cremated; his eyes and his prayer beads were not consumed by the flames.
His relics were interred at the mountain monastery, and half of them were enshrined in a stupa on Mount Xiufeng. Initially, Zhen Dianxiong had surpassed all others in his resolve.
His unrestrained demeanor was transcendent and free-flowing; yet, when it came to inheriting the Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*), he stood firm like a jade pillar, lofty and imposing.
His practice was profound and his conduct sublime. Throughout his life, he never wore silk garments, and for more than forty years, his ribs did not touch his mat.

When the Master succeeded to that Way, he was even more rigorous in disciplining himself. Regarding the regulations of the monastic community, there were those which other quarters were unable to practice, yet the Master—
He was simple and frugal; during his lifetime he did not accumulate surplus goods, and at his death he possessed not even a complete set of robes.

Should anyone wish to seek from him formal vestments or titles of honor, he would decline them, saying, "Even if you were to bring them here, they would only suffice to serve as a pillow for the light of day.
His dharma discourses and verses were profound and weighty in expression, possessing the refined style of a true master.
The commentary states: When Xiu Peak was first at Lingjiu, while he was still a youth, he heard two venerable elders conversing at night.

They cited a verse by an ancient master that said: "The rattle of the chariot wheels passes over the South of the River; For a time, this humble body is lodged at Letan. The mist and sands of Mount Qin have not yet subsided;

Under the bright moon, the meditation hut of the monk remains locked empty. Upon hearing this, he was immediately moved to realization and wept. When the elders asked him the reason for his tears, [he explained his insight].
He replied, "I obtained this verse within a dream; it must have been the result of my past lives. An elder said, "If this is truly so, you will surely become the master of Letan in the future.
Later, Xiufeng fled from Letan to Tiantai, where he eventually passed away at the hermitage of National Teacher Shao.
Indeed, it was just as he had said. The teachings state that all realms of retribution are produced by the power of past habits and vows.

Manifesting this, he demonstrates that there is a fixed portion [of destiny]; how could it not be so? The world, driven by common folly, competes in petty pursuits, seeking only to conform to the trivialities of fame and profit;
though some may even die for such things, none find peace in their proper station. Upon hearing of the influence of Xiufeng, they will surely be moved.
This is all the more cause for shame.
Zen Master Yunju Wu was named Shanwu.
He was born into the Li clan and was a native of Xingdao in Yangzhou. Having left the household life, he recited the sutras and received ordination.

He was fully ordained and possessed innate wisdom and keen intelligence. Initially, upon hearing Chan Master Chong cite the words of Bodhidharma, "Vast and empty, there is no sage," he immediately said, "Since I am already vast and empty, what sage could there be? Chong marveled at these words and sent him south on a pilgrimage.
He traveled extensively through the regions of Shu and Qi, visiting and questioning various masters of the school. Upon reaching Longmen, he met Chan Master Fuyan, who cited a saying of Yunmen.
[The Master] said: "To reach the point where mountains, rivers, and the great earth are free from even the slightest flaw is still a 'turning phrase' (*zhuǎnjù*).

Not seeing a single form is only half the presentation. Only when you further know there is the 'full presentation' (*quántí*) can you truly attain it. The Master’s mind reached a resonance with this, and he accordingly took him as his teacher.
One night, Fuyan said to him: "Have you heard of the solitary pheasant dancing in pairs? In the past, there were two pheasants that would always dance together. Once..."
One of its companions was lost; it stopped and no longer danced. A wise man held a mirror up to it; seeing its own reflection, the solitary pheasant immediately began to dance.
The Master attained sudden enlightenment. One day, as a cat passed before him carrying a mouse, Fo-yen pointed to it and showed it to the Master. The Master said:
Mount Huánggōng collapsed. Fǎyǎn rejoiced at this and consequently ordered him to share his seat and preach the Dharma. Once, citing the occasion of Dēshān’s night assembly, he said:
"When Wù Zhàoshàng was asked a question tonight, he did not answer. If a monk had stepped forward, he would have simply said:
'Where have you been for all this time? Fǎyǎn moved with emotion and said: "From now on, I shall sleep with my head high. From that time forth, it was thus.

His reputation spread in all four directions. At the beginning of the Xuande era, he appeared in the world at Tianning Monastery in Jizhou; the following year, he moved to Yunju in Nan’gang. His school’s style flourished greatly.

The Master was by nature square and stern; his words were not uttered lightly. He followed the example of the assembly with his own person; even during freezing cold or scorching heat, he would invariably join the community.
When lying down at night beneath a three-beamed structure, if there were those who were indolent or failed to rise at the proper time, he would invariably strike his pillow to rouse them.
He cautioned [his disciples]. All the utensils for the abbot’s personal use were merely displayed as formalities; he never actually made use of them. He styled himself "Gao'an" (High Hermitage).
At that time, Chan Master Letan Xiang was also highly distinguished and established his own reputation; in general, his virtue and prestige were equal to those of the Master.

However, in terms of enduring ascetic discipline and winning over the assembly, the Master surpassed him. After seven years had passed, Chan Master Yuanwu received the imperial decree to reside [at Mount Dahui].

At Yunju, there was an imperial decree to transfer the Master to Jingshan; he firmly declined on account of illness. The following year, Yuanwu returned to Sichuan, and the Governor of Nanchang again invited the Master to Yunju.
Shortly thereafter, due to military turmoil, he declined the offer and departed. He sought refuge in Tiantai and took up residence at the hermitage of National Teacher Shao.
In the second year of the Shaoxing era, the Prefect of Taizhou received an imperial edict to convert Fushan Hongfu Temple into a Chan monastery, and [the Master] was selected for this post.

There was a man of great virtue who accepted the invitation. The Prefect used his influence to entreat the Master; the Master firmly declined. The Prefect then petitioned the court, and in the sixth month, the imperial decree arrived.
Reluctantly, the Master consented. At that time, there were still several hundred disciples who followed him, carrying their own provisions.
One day, he recounted the circumstances of the World-Honored One’s final entry into parinirvāṇa and his display of the *svastika* on his chest.

He opened his robe and said to the assembly, "Behold this with full satisfaction; do not let yourselves regret it later. Then he said, "I am old now. Shall I return to the three pagodas of my native mountain?
A monk asked, "But what of Mount Fushan, which you have just taken charge of? The Master replied, "Can one remain as abbot merely because of death?"
The monk asked, "When may I depart? The Master said, "Wait until someone comes along carrying straw sandals, then you shall go.
The monk asked, "May I go as well? The Master said, "If you know how to stick out your beak, then you may. The monk replied, "Yes, yes. The Master smiled and let it rest.

On the first day of the seventh month, the attendant hurriedly prepared for his departure. The Master did not don his traveling robes. The next day, having risen from his midday nap, he spoke as usual; then, suddenly, he waved his hand.
The attendant monk said, "Go, go. The monk withdrew. After waiting a short while, he found that [the master] had already passed away while sitting in the lotus posture.
He had lived for fifty-nine years and spent forty-one summer retreats in formal residence. His sacred remains and śarīra relics were divided, with one portion enshrined in the three stupas at Yunju.
First, he was buried at Fushan and enshrined as the founding patriarch.
As for Chan Master Baiyang Shun, his name was Fashun.
He was the son of the Wen family from Weicheng in Mianzhou. When he was seven or eight years old, in the darkness of night...

He perceived things as if it were broad daylight. His parents, recognizing his extraordinary nature, caused him to leave the household life. He received the full precepts (ordination) under the patronage of Xianglin Temple.
Traveling to Chengdu, he followed Master Chongwu of Daci Temple to receive instruction in the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra*.

When he reached the passage stating, "To be free from thought is called 'attaining entry,'" he studied it with great intensity for a long time. Holding this point, he questioned Master Wu, who hesitated and was unable to resolve his doubts.

He then encouraged him to travel to study under various masters, and he went to attend upon Chan Master Jingjue of Guyin. During the Daguan era, Fuyan resided at Longmen, where his reputation for the Way was widespread;
[Wuzhun] went to rely upon him. For many years, he served with utmost sincerity and underwent all manner of menial tasks without ever showing a trace of weariness.

One night, while hearing the mention that the flavor of salt exists within water and the color of glue exists within blue pigment—certainly they exist, yet their forms are not seen—he suddenly attained a realization.
Thereupon, he transcended discursive thought and grasped the essential principle of "entering," attaining a profound and seamless resonance with it.
The next day, when entering the inner quarters, Longmen asked him, "Where is the True Buddha? The Master replied, "He is in an indeterminate place. Longmen said, "Since he is the True Buddha, why..."
"Extremely indeterminate. The Master said, "If it were determinate, it would not be the true Buddha. Longmen found this strange and asked, "How did you reach such a state?
The Master told him the truth. Longmen questioned him further, saying, "The flavor of salt in water; the lacquer-blue within the color—how do you directly comprehend this?
The Master replied, "There is no need for further comprehension. Longmen approved of this. From then on, their exchanges were like rolling thunder and falling rain.
The multitude gazed upon him with awe. After Longmen passed away and his *śarīra* had been enshrined in a stupa, he immediately became the head of the monastic community at Yunju.
He shared the teaching seat with others and welcomed fellow practitioners; before he had even had time to sweep the hall, the doorsteps were filled with the shoes of visitors.

At the beginning of the Jianyan era, an imperial decree was issued that all temples serving as sites for the Shenxiao cult should revert to their former status as Buddhist monasteries. Thereupon, the Transport Commissioner, Lord Zhang Cong, [acted accordingly].
He was the first to open Guangshou Temple in Linchuan and invited the Master to establish the Dharma there. In the first year of the Xiangxing era, Magistrate Jiang Xuanqing moved him to Baiyang.
There were only old buildings with a few pillars that could not even shelter one from wind and rain; previously, the resident monks had been extravagant and negligent.
The temple relied on these offerings for its sustenance. Upon the Master’s arrival, he struck it down at once. He then became greatly inspired and achieved many great deeds.
Before a year had passed, his reputation spread far and wide, and he was revered by all; monks rushed toward him with all their might, arriving like surging clouds.
The Master did not rise from his seat; he transformed a humble and dilapidated dwelling into a precious monastery (*ratnavihāra*).

In his daily life, he was tirelessly devoted to receiving people, providing instruction and conducting interrogations without interruption, even in moments of haste. By nature, he was upright and resolute, refusing to conform to worldly customs.
When discussing the Way, he did not hesitate to offer criticism or rebuke. Someone once asked: "Under the gate of Dongshan, Foguo was solitary and austere, while Foyan was compassionate and gentle."
"What are the coarse and fine qualities of what these two have attained? The Master assumed a stern expression and said, "Fashun saw his father coming in the midst of a bustling marketplace.
For you to ask about softness, hardness, coarseness, and fineness—is this not a mistake? His analysis of doubts and shattering of delusions was often like this.
He once addressed the assembly, saying, "From dawn until dusk, this mountain monk’s hands and feet have never ceased moving; I have been on the eastern corridor..."
Passing through the western corridor and the Buddha Hall, they again traverse the three sections of the kitchen and storehouse.
The Master carries firewood while two craftsmen pull the saw—even the Buddha cannot manage it. Having no way to comprehend this, how am I to provide a commentary?
He reveals the eyes of Bodhidharma and opens the gateway of the white poplar tree. The assembly need not further don the robe of Zhaozhou; beneath it, one must strip away the mother.
Shengkuo. Li Boji, the Regional Commander of Jiangxi, admired his Way and desired to have an audience with him. He sent a formal request through Huanglong, and the messenger arrived twice.
The Master remained lying firm in bed and did not go. On the first day of the fifth month of the ninth year, he assembled the congregation to bid them farewell.
The attendant held paper and requested a verse. The Master said, "My usual talk has already been abundant; what more need be said now?
He then instructed his attendants, "Report to me this evening as soon as the cock crows. Shortly thereafter, he suddenly heard the bell signaling the end of meditation.
He then let out a great shout. His attendants looked on in astonishment; he was already sitting in the full lotus posture, having passed away. He had lived for sixty-four years. Sitting...
He spent forty-six years in the rainy-season retreats. Among the remains of the cremation, his eyeballs, teeth, tongue, and cranial bone were not consumed by the fire, as was the rosary he held;

his relics were of five colors. A stupa was erected at the western corner of the monastery. Although the Master appeared physically unassuming and of ordinary stature, his spiritual bearing was clear and transcendent.
His conduct was firm and upright, and he was skilled in composing verses, which he would produce spontaneously at the brush’s tip.

Having already established a distinguished reputation and seeing that his Way was flourishing and far from exhausted, he suddenly passed away. Monks from all quarters, whether they knew him personally or not, were so moved by grief that they could not help but shed tears.
Such was the way he won the hearts of people.
The eulogy states: Xu Gong Shichuan, the Grand Secretary for Confidential Matters, said: "Excellent! Master Daoshi possesses the clear eye, and his steady gait is truly worthy of its name;
both feet and eyes have reached their destination. Thus, Ga’ān is the elder brother and Bǎiyáng is the younger brother."

Truly profound are these words. Upon careful observation, we see that Gao’an Yan presided over a great monastery, humbling himself and applying his strength to the Way, treating the assembly as his own kin.
In desolate villages with white poplars and ruined temples, he rose up with vigor and determination, and his fame surpassed that of his contemporaries. Thus, both masters propagated the Dharma.
Not even ten years had passed, yet every word of his teachings and conduct remains such that one can still visualize his very countenance even after a hundred generations.

Alas! He perished by following the Way; this was the consequence of his private integrity. Compared to those of other times who relied on their power to commit excesses and wickedness, carving at others to serve themselves—how different are they from mere dung and soil?
*The Continued Biographies of the Sangha Jewel*, Scroll Four;
*The Continued Biographies of the Sangha Jewel*, Scroll Five.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zuxiu of Longxing Prefecture.

Chan Master Baofeng Qing, whose name was Shanqing, was born into the He clan in Baochang, Nanxiong. He relied upon Fae’en of Xianglin Temple, where he underwent his studies, received ordination, and attained full precepts.
At the age of thirty, he first began his travels to seek teachers, eventually relying upon Chan Master Huanglong Huaitang.

After a long time, he attained enlightenment and presented a verse. Huìtáng said, "Attaining the Way is easy; guarding the Way is difficult. Guarding the Way still depends on oneself, but preaching the Dharma for others is difficult.
In a single phrase of our school, there are three mysteries; in each mystery, there are three essentials.
There are mysteries and there are essentials—look into this yourself hereafter. The Master then composed another verse, which included the lines: "In every land, in every atom, I offer this..."
Huitang approved the phrase "the body. [The Master] then departed to travel through Jiang and Zhejiang, visiting and questioning various patriarchs.
Upon returning to Mount Lu, he went to see Chan Master Zhenjing, who asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From down the Yangtze River. Zhenjing said, "What have you brought back?

He replied, "What do you want, Master? Zhenjing said, "I want everything. The Master lifted up his sitting cloth (*zuoju*). Zhenjing said, "That is just furniture for leisure. The Master said, "Indeed."
"Do not be so hasty," [Dongshan] said. Jing replied, "Try bringing it forth for me to see. The Master struck his sitting mat once. Jing was struck with wonder and amazement.
When Sijian Huizang (Sixin) appeared in the world, Lingyuan sent a letter inviting him to serve as his assistant. Master Sixin marveled at him, saying, "He is of vast fortune, mature, and resolute;
he possesses a rigorous and discerning capacity. Whenever Sixin moved from Cuiyan to reside again at Yunyan, and subsequently transferred to Huanglong, [Jing] accompanied him.
The masters were all present there, and [Dahui] usually occupied the first seat. Sharing the dais and receiving the patch-robes, he associated with Sishi (Sijian) for nearly twenty years.
His learning was profound and extensive, and his wit and eloquence were peerless. In the fifth year of the Zhenghe era, Sishi passed away.

Grand Master Zhang Sicheng invited the Master to succeed him on the seat, where he propagated the Dharma and sang the Way of Huitang. At that time, Huanglong was renowned as a great master of the Dharma.
The monks in the cave were all extraordinary and eminent men. The Master ascended the hall and said: "Yesterday, I was a guest in the forest; today, I am the abbot upon the dais.
To let go or to gather, it is entirely up to me; amidst the myriad phenomena, my body alone is revealed.

The following year, he resigned from his duties at the monastery and built a thatched hut beside it, calling himself "Cao Tang" (Thatched Hall). After some time, he returned to reside there once more. Ascending the hall, he said: "Close [the door]..."
He spent six winters at Ximutang. With his mind forgotten and the objective realm stilled, the myriad conditions were empty. He did not know from where illusory karma arose;
as before, he continued to uphold the teachings and revitalize the ancestral wind. At the end of the Jianyan era, he sought refuge in Linchuan.

The Prefect Jiang Xuanqing invited him to reside at Caoshan, and later he moved to Shushan. In the fifth year of the Shaoxing era, having retired from monastic affairs, he entrusted the temple matters to his Dharma heir, Liaru.
The Chan Master then retired to live in seclusion; yet he never grew weary of receiving visitors, and students flocked to him, fearing only to be late.

His reputation for the Way soon became preeminent in the world. When Governor Zhang, the Minister of State of Nanchang, heard of his fame, he was delighted but lamented that he could not bring the Master to him.

It so happened that Xu Shan, the Grand Secretary of the Imperial Chancellery, passed through Hongzhou; together they offered to vacate Lestan Monastery to invite the Master. At that time, the Master was eighty years old.
There were three [invitations]. He declined them with great firmness, yet they pressed him with increasing courtesy.
Unable to refuse, he went. The Great Master proceeded to the East Mountain in the prefecture at their request; the entire city flocked to witness him, marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence.

When he resided at Lestam, his students disciplined themselves without being exhorted and practiced virtue without being transformed. Before a year had passed, his reputation was vast and unsurpassed.
There were five thousand distinguished monks who had come from distant lands. Since the rise of the military campaigns, no forest monastery had ever been as flourishing as this.
On the final day of the first month in the twelfth year, he took out his robes and bowl, sang the *gāthā* of entrustment, and settled his final affairs.
The following day, he sat upright and passed away. He had lived in the world for eighty-six years and spent sixty summer retreats in meditation. After his cremation, his eyeballs remained unburnt.
After his passing, his spirit-bones and *śarīra* relics were enshrined in a stupa at Huanglong. Whenever he spoke of worldly affairs to distinguished guests, he would stare with wide-open eyes;

after a long while, he would say in a stern voice, "This old monk’s hearing is dull. Yet when receiving students for private instruction or responding to their inquiries, his exchanges were as swift as a lightning strike or a shooting star.
Even those who were beginners dared not question him further, yet he never showed the slightest sign of weariness. It was as if...
He recited one entire collection of the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* every day. Such was his method for propagating the Way that he remained increasingly diligent even in old age.
Chan Master Da-mei Guo, whose name was Shanguo, was the son of the Yu family of Yanshan in Xin Prefecture; he received the full precepts under Yuanjia of Qibao Monastery.
He was fully endowed with the precepts. His Brahmanic features were extraordinary and ancient; his forehead was broad and his nose prominent. From his youth, he admired the Way of the Patriarchs.
When he first arrived at Goose Lake (E’u), he sat in meditative repose within the Zen hall. He heard two children playing and disputing over a meditation cushion (*pútán*).

One of them picked it up and said, "You say you do not see this; what is it? At these words, the Master attained a sudden realization. Later, while traveling to Cloud Abode (Yúnjū), a Zen practitioner happened to arrive from Yellow Dragon (Huánglóng).
He asked the old master Sīxin, "What kind of words do you always use when engaging with people? The Chan practitioner replied, "I often cite Yunmen’s question to a monk:
'The luminous, tranquil illumination pervades the sands of the Ganges—is this not the speech of the scholar Zhang Zhuo?
The monk said, 'It is. Yunmen said, 'Your talk has fallen. Where, then, does the talk fall? Upon hearing this, the Master attained a sudden and great awakening; he immediately went to Huangbo.

Longmen could have been entrusted to Sishi, who declined the post and directed him to see Kefu Ning Daozhe. When the Master arrived at Kefu, there was a profound accord between master and disciple; Ning marveled at him deeply.
He invited the Master to reside in the library at that time, when there were five thousand monks at Kefu.

As Ning approached his passing, he alone conferred his fly-whisk upon the Master; the details of this account are found in the biography of Ning. Having received this final entrustment, the Master lived in seclusion.

At Jidao Temple, when Chan Master Huanyu arrived to preside over the seat, he had heard much of the Master’s reputation. One night, he offered half of his seat to him and requested that he preach the Dharma.
The Master raised the koan of Qianfeng regarding the Dharmakāya; his analysis was so transcendent that it went beyond the reach of the intellect.

Huanyu marveled at this for a long time. From then on, the Master’s reputation for the Way grew even more prominent. At the beginning of the Xuande era, the official Cen Xiaoxu of Tanzhou invited him to appear in the world.
Seal. *The Essential Teachings of Gongkānggong*. At that time, the Dharma seat of Chan Master Longya Cai was quite flourishing;
whenever he answered questions, he frequently used the term "sulū. One day, he joined several elders at the banquet of the Provincial Commander, Lord Zeng.
The Lord asked, "When Longya answers questions, he always says 'sulū. What is the meaning of this? The elders looked at one another, and none could respond. The Master stepped forward.
Taking his seat, he stepped forward and said, "I have just had a certain remark; Master, please clarify it for me. The Master said, "Longya’s answer was merely 'Sulu.
Do you all understand? Last night, space opened its mouth and laughed: "Zhurong has swallowed Lake Dongting!

Lord Zeng was greatly delighted, and the entire assembly leaned forward in admiration. Subsequently, Daoxuan was appointed to Daling and Daowu to Fuyan, where the school's influence flourished most vibrantly.
His Dharma seat was always preeminent among all regions. Within his quarters, he was exquisite in his manner of receiving people.

He frequently cited the story of the scholar Zhang Zhuo from Yunmen to test his students; in his spontaneous bestowal or withholding of instruction, no one could fathom its origins. The world held him in universal esteem.

He styled himself Yue’an (Moon Hermitage), and many officials and literati from Xiangzhong followed him to inquire about the Way. In the ninth year of the Shaoxing era, Lord Zhang, the State Councilor...
When De-yuan governed the Seven Min Provinces, he invited the Master to reside at Gushan. Before he could arrive, the invitation was changed to Huangbo;

subsequently, the Master moved between the two Chan centers of Dong and Xi. After ten years, he grew somewhat weary of the local customs of Min and his heart inclined toward the regions beyond the Yangtze.

Many monastics gathered around him, and as the seats at Wannian in Tai, Shuanglin in Wuzhou, and Daopei in Tan were all vacant, the three prefectures vied to invite him, with Changsha being the most persistent. The Master...
He said, "Tán was a place where I used to travel; I delighted in it. He then accepted the summons to Dàméi.

On the eighteenth day of the first month of the twenty-second year, he brought forth his robes and bowl and entrusted them to his attendants. He commissioned the making of images of the five hundred arhats.

The following day, he bathed, changed his clothes, and gathered the assembly to bid them farewell. He wrote a gāthā by hand, saying: "If one wishes to go, one simply goes; if one wishes to leave, one simply leaves. *Zhuàng*..."

He shattered the celestial gates and overturned the earth’s axis. He passed away with his brush still held, having lived seventy-four years in this world and spent fifty-one summer retreats in meditation.

His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the Western Peak of Weiyuan. By nature the Master was upright and firm; he lived simply and frugally while governing the monastic community with strict clarity.

Whenever he moved to a major monastery, it was always at the invitation of eminent officials and high-ranking dignitaries of the age who humbled themselves to entreat him; the monastic communities were all in awe of him.
He attained the pinnacle of human excellence.
The eulogy says: Caotang obtained the functional activity of Sīxīn and did not forget Huìtáng;
Yuè’ān heard Sīxīn’s words and attained enlightenment, thereby entering the chamber of Master Níng. Thus, the lineage of Sīxīn was ultimately not continued—how regrettable! Nevertheless, Caotang...
When he first emerged from Longshan and moved to Baiyun, the world was beset by many hardships and he had not yet achieved significant results.

However, when he later resided at Letan, his Way flourished greatly before his passing, whereby he ultimately revitalized the ancestral style throughout the land; thus, the instruction of Huitang to propagate the Way was fulfilled.
After Yue’an entered the monastic order, more than thirty years passed; he moved through eight major monasteries and never for a single day remained in retirement.
Beneath the striking of the whisk, his retinue has always numbered several thousand; how efficacious was the transmission of the *zhuchi* (dust-whisk) at Kaifu!
The *I Ching* says, "Observe one's conduct to examine the auspicious. I have found this truth in the moment of transmission between these two elders, father and son.
Chan Master Huguo Yuan, whose name was Jingyuan, was the son of the Zhang family from Nanxi in Yongjia. He relied upon Xigong at Lingshan Monastery;

at the age of eighteen, he received the tonsure and became a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*). He studied the teachings of the Tiantai school and mastered their doctrines, but subsequently abandoned them to travel widely, eventually visiting Jiangshan.
One day, Chan Master Yuanwu heard a nearby monk cite the words from Sishin’s *Small Public Sermon*, which said: "Since one is deluded, one must attain awakening;

since one has awakened, one must recognize delusion within awakening and awakening within delusion. When both delusion and awakening are forgotten, one establishes all dharmas from the state where there is neither delusion nor awakening.
He savored these words for a long time. Then, while rising to walk, he suddenly attained a breakthrough realization. Immediately—

He reported this to Yuanwu, who was pleased by it. Consequently, he was accepted as an attendant. For fourteen years, he engaged in inquiry and consultation until his realization was perfectly clear and uninterrupted;
his spiritual acuity was so preeminent that the assembly nicknamed him "Nao-tou" (The Stubborn Head).
When Yuanwu was about to return to Sichuan, he suddenly asked, "In the future, if someone asks you, what will you say? The Master patted the back of a nearby monk.

The Master said, "Upādhyāya, why did you not answer him? Yuanwu laughed heartily. Shortly thereafter, he took a *mu-jin* (wood-cotton) *saṃghāṭī* from his sleeve and presented it to him before departing.

At the beginning of the Xiangxing era, he returned to live in seclusion at his former monastery. The Provincial Governor of Kuochang, Dragon-Scholar Geng Yanxi, appointed him to the abbacy of Renshou, followed by Lianyun.
In his later years, he resided at Zhenru and subsequently moved to Huguo. Monastic disciples flocked to follow him, and his Dharma...

The assembly grew increasingly large. The Master’s preaching of the Dharma transcended conventional categories; his discernment was beyond all paths. A student asked, "I have come here to request an audience with the Master.
The Master said, "Understood. What is this matter of having an audience? The student asked, "How is it that you see me? The Master said, "Your eyes are on the left and on the right.
The student pressed further, "In that case, when all functions cease, the True Eye opens. The Master said, "The bright sun is in the sky."

"Blind men feeling their way along the ground. [A monk] asked, "What is it like when you have met [the Buddha] and what is it like when you have not yet met him? The Master said, "At once they are pierced through.

[The monk] asked, "If a superior person of the highest caliber were to suddenly encounter you, what then? The Master said, "I would set them out beneath the three-legged seat. [The monk] asked, "Do you permit a student to take this up and carry it forth?
The Master said, "The army follows the seal. [The monk] asked, "What is the Linji school? The Master said, "The army follows the seal."
The Master said, "To kill or to give life without blinking an eye. [The student] asked, "What is the Yunmen school?
The Master said, "Three eyes in the crown of the head illuminate heaven and earth. [The student] asked, "What is the Guiyang school? The Master said, "Pushed forward, he does not go forward;
pulled back, he does not retreat. [The student] asked, "What is the Fayan school? The Master said, "The tips of arrows meet, neither yielding to the other. [The student] asked, "How is it..."
"What is this Cao-Dong school? The Master said, "Holding a night-bright talisman in hand, how many know when the dawn breaks?
[The monk] asked, "Is there still a path beyond? The Master said, "There is. [The monk] asked, "What is the path beyond? The Master said, "A vast expanse of blackness.
[The monk] asked, "When one respectfully bows to Śākyamuni and does not pay homage to Maitreya, what then? The Master said, "Wait until you have received thirty blows of the staff."
At another time, when the monks were performing prostrations, the Master said: "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still his slaves. Tell me, who is he?

It is true that he is Huguo (Guarding the Nation), yet this is not so. Sitting and standing with solemn dignity, crowning heaven and treading upon the earth—whenever one bumps into him or brushes against him throughout the twelve periods of the day, who is it? Do you know? Exert yourself! You must bring this to completion in this very life."
Do not let yourself suffer through the cycles of delusion for countless kalpas. He inscribed a verse for the *Rushi Xuan* (Suchness Pavilion) as follows: "Cast aside Gautama’s idle proclamations;
Uproot the tangles of the patriarchs. Simply hang 'Thus' across the pavilion; Even those with iron brows and copper heads can do nothing against it.
He presented a verse for the practitioners of Chan as follows: "To seek realization at the tip of the staff requires effort; To accept it under a shout is not yet remarkable."
He turned the true eye of the ancestral school upon the crown of his head, teaching that even Buddhas and Patriarchs must humble their waves.

On the ninth day of the first month of the sixteenth year, he passed away due to a slight illness. He was interred at his home mountain; he was fifty-three years of age and had thirty-five years of ordination seniority.
His disciples were numerous and flourishing, such that he resembled the Monk with the Cloth Bag depicted in the world; therefore, people called him by that name.
He profoundly mastered the functional pivot of Yuanwu and practiced it with vigor. The world was just beginning to look up to him, having heard of his refined character;
unfortunately, he passed away prematurely, a fact lamented by those who discussed him.
Chan Master Yunju Ru: The Chan Master’s name was Faju.
He was the son of the Hu family of Linhai in Taizhou. Having relied upon Chan Master Rui of Huguo Temple, he shaved his head and received full ordination.

He traveled extensively to study under the masters of the various schools throughout the two provinces of Zhejiang. Hearing that Chan Master Fuyan resided at Longmen and that his reputation for the Way was exceedingly great, he went there to seek instruction.

He traveled from more than a thousand *li* away to visit him. He presented his understanding, gained through diligent effort, and asked Fo-yen to verify it. Fo-yen said, "All of this is merely intellectual learning; it is not the ultimate matter.
If you wish to resolve the cycle of birth and death, you must seek wondrous enlightenment. The Master was struck with awe and accepted these words with deep conviction.

After one day, Fo-yen appointed him as the steward (*dianzuo*), but the Master firmly declined on the grounds that his spiritual practice was not yet complete. Fo-yen encouraged him, saying, "For now..."
He took up a position. Among those there was a person of great capacity who preached the Dharma for him.

Not long after, as he rose at dawn and opened the kitchen door, he caught sight of the Holy Monk (Śākyamuni) and attained a sudden realization. He went inside and saw Foyan, who asked, "Do you see the Holy Monk here?
The Master stood before him with palms joined in greeting. Foyan nodded his head and said, "I told you there was a person of great capacity here for you."
He preached the Dharma. On another occasion, he asked, "The Stone Bridge at Tiantai has collapsed during the night. The Master immediately seized Foyan. Foyan said, "What?
The Master replied, "And you say the Stone Bridge has collapsed. Foyan deeply approved of this.
Later, when the Master entered the quarters of Chan Master Yuanwu, he asked, "Have you been studying only with Foyan, or have you seen other teachers as well? The Master replied, "I have also..."
Once, when someone came, [Gao'an] asked, "Who is this person? The Master pointed to his chest and said, "Faru.
Yuanwu said, "What you have seen is but a mere spark. The Master replied, "It is already much.

Later, Chan Master Gao'an Wuxin and Yuanwu succeeded one another as abbots of Yunju, both of whom deferred to the Master as the First Seat (Dizuo) and shared the seat with him to receive monastic students.

He was treated with great affection. At the beginning of the Jianyan era, the seat at Shanglan Monastery was vacant; the regional commander Hu Zhiru commanded him to appear in the world and propagate the teachings of Foyan.
Before long, the barbarian cavalry approached the city walls, so he went into seclusion at Baishui Hermitage. It happened that Yunju Monastery had been reduced to ashes by the fires of war.

At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, the abbacy was changed four times, yet each incumbent fled due to the hardships of the times. When the Provincial Transport Commissioner, Lord Zeng Yu, entrusted the monastery to the Master, the patriarchal style of the school flourished greatly.
The Master’s insight and capacity were profound and vast; his spiritual agility was like that of a deity, such that all who saw him were struck with awe and submission.

Dayang secretly transmitted to him the essential principles of the Caodong school. Subsequently, he traveled to the Eastern Capital. In the sixth year of the Xuandao era, Yuanwu—
The Chan Master received the imperial decree and went to Tianning Monastery in the capital. He rejoiced to himself, saying, "Heaven has granted me the opportunity to meet this old man;
I shall not fail the intent of Master Zhantang Zhang’s guidance. He then proceeded to Tianning, where he listened to the essential teachings of the Dharma as they were delivered from the high seat.
This was entirely different from what he had heard on ordinary days, and he immediately devoted himself to him with total sincerity. After forty days had passed, Yuanwu raised the question:
"When a monk asked Yunmen, 'What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? Yunmen replied, 'On the waters above the mountain to the east. If someone were to ask Tianning, I would simply say:
'A fragrant breeze comes from the south; the halls and pavilions grow cool. At these words, [Tianning] attained sudden enlightenment.

Upon hearing of his sudden enlightenment, Yuanwu was greatly pleased and moved Master [Wuzu] to the Zhemu Hall. There, he subjected him to rigorous training through the various causes and conditions of the past and present.
One day, while Yuanwu was eating, the layman Zhao Churao sat with him; suddenly, the Master forgot to lift his chopsticks.

"Why did you fail today? The Master asked. "The entire great earth is this very thing; how do you see it, Upāsaka Gao? The man was speechless.

The Dharma assembly flourished daily, and the school’s teaching style was greatly revitalized; he was hailed as the restorer of the Linji lineage.

He then collected the recorded sayings and karmic conditions (*jīyuán*) of the former virtuous masters, interspersing...

Consequently, the local residents were moved toward conversion, and some went so far as to paint his portrait and offer sacrifices with food and drink whenever they ate.

In the winter of the year Yihai, he received imperial grace and returned north. In the spring of the following year, he was restored to his status as a monk (*saṃghāṭī*). Shortly thereafter, he received an imperial decree and took up residence in Mingzhou.
At Mount Yuyang, more than a year later, an imperial decree was issued for him to reside at Mount Jing. The eminent monks from all under heaven gathered there once again as before.

At that time, His Majesty, while still in the status of a crown prince, had long heard of the Master’s reputation. He dispatched an Inner Palace Supervisor to the mountain to inquire about the essential meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
When the Master ascended the hall, he spoke this verse: "The eye atop the head is wide open, Illuminating the entire great trichiliocosm. Since I am the King within the Dharma,"
He attained mastery over the Dharma and offered this verse in tribute: "Great root, great vessel, and great power; you shoulder the Great Matter in a manner most extraordinary.
A single hair-tip conveys the news; throughout the entire world, all is manifest and unrevealed. The Emperor praised him for a long time.
He then established a residence for him and dispatched an inner attendant to enter the mountains to provide offerings to five hundred arhats and to invite the Master.
He preached the Dharma and personally inscribed the large characters for "Myōki-an" (Wondrous Joy Hermitage), composing a eulogy which he sent with special favor, saying:

"Birth and extinction are neither extinguished; permanence and dwelling are not abiding. Perfect enlightenment is empty and luminous, manifesting according to objects. When the Master ascended the hall, he spoke this verse:
"The entire dharma-realm reaches the person's mouth; all that exists within the dharma-realm is his tongue. Relying solely upon this mouth and tongue, I offer my prayers for you."
May Your Majesty’s life be without interruption; for ten million years and more, may the source of blessings flow forth. Like the surging ocean, its mercury shall never be exhausted.
From within the Lion’s Den, the *śarabha* and the *jīvañjīvaka* shall surely emerge from the Cinnabar Mountains. As auspicious omens and portents, they shall pervade the nine realms of the earth.
The grasses, trees, insects, and all creatures were filled with joy; they bowed their heads in reverence to this inconceivable event.
Just as the myriad stars surround the bright moon, I now proclaim these wondrous verses, speaking the truth within the context of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).

As my teacher had reached an advanced age and sought to retire from the monastery, in the spring of the *xin-si* year, he received imperial permission to withdraw and reside in the Bright Moon Hall (*Mingyue-tang*) of the temple. Nevertheless, he continued to propagate the Dharma for the sake of others.
Even in old age, he never grew weary. When the Emperor ascended the throne, he was specially granted the title of Chan Master Dahui.

During the Xianyun era of the Longxing period, on the eve of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, a star fell to the west of the monastery; its radiance was brilliant and its sound like thunder. The Master manifested a slight illness.
On the ninth day of the eighth month, when his disciples came to inquire after him, he exhorted them to propagate the Way. He then dismissed them slowly, saying: "I..."

The journey commenced the following day. At the fifth watch, he personally wrote his final testament. His attendant monk earnestly requested that he leave behind a verse of farewell, so he wrote four lines.
He then cast aside his brush and retired to bed, passing away in profound stillness. He was seventy-five years of age. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa behind the hall.
Subsequently, an imperial decree designated his residence as Miaoxi Hermitage; he was posthumously titled Pujue, and his stupa was named Baoguang. The Master had borne the Buddha’s...
The Patriarch’s direct succession is the total manifestation of function; it sweeps away all views and conceptions, leaving no dharma to be given to others.
Even the ancient masters could add nothing to this. Indeed, in his unimpeded eloquence and his ability to harmonize the various teachings, he fully embodied the style of Yuanwu.
Therefore, his lofty and majestic gateways accommodated and gathered a vast multitude; like the ocean containing all and the earth bearing all, he was capacious and had more than enough room.

As for his use of staffs and shouts, sarcasm and rebukes, jesting and laughter, or even angry scoldings—none were anything other than the total presentation of the Ultimate Teaching to receive and guide others.
It is simply that students find it difficult to find a foothold therein. His broad-minded magnanimity and freedom from restrictive constraints caused disciples everywhere to hasten to serve him.

Although there were those who had already emerged with prominent talents and were hailed as leaders throughout the various quarters, the Master directed them to investigate the profound mysteries as if they were his own attendants.
His poetic eulogies, verses on ancient cases, and correspondence with worthy scholars and gentlemen discussing the Way,
along with his formal sermons and general discourses on the Dharma, comprise five fascicles that have been circulated in the world.
The commentary states: In recent times, Master Lü Gongjuren once remarked that Zhaozhou’s teaching of Chan was like the military tactics of Xiang Yu:
proceeding directly forward without leaving a trace, breaking whatever stood before him and subduing whatever he encountered.

It was not like other teachers who weigh and measure with precision down to the *zhu* and *cun*, only then considering themselves to have attained success. When I observe Dahui’s teaching of Chan, it is likewise...

That those who dwell in benevolence call him "Zhaozhou" is indeed correct. Since the time of the patriarchs in the Middle Kingdom, there have been those who have thoroughly fathomed the source of the Dharma and possessed the power of total mastery, appearing side by side with the ancestral masters; such individuals have not been lacking from generation to generation.

Yet, as for one whose gate of awakening is vast and expansive, who delights in the unimpeded eloquence of free speech, and whose realization is so profound and overflowing, is Master Dahui not truly a rare talent appearing only once in an interval between ages? How magnificent he is!
His methods for responding to the capacities of his disciples were versatile: capable of being lavish or frugal, arduous or easy, permissive or restrictive;
every response was consummate, and every teaching was fresh. This is why his influence spread throughout the world and his fame reached the imperial court;
it is no exaggeration to call him the "Restorer of Linji. Not long after his passing, his reputation for the Dharma shone even more brightly, and his dharma heirs flourished daily.
Among those who study Chan throughout the world, they look up to him as to Mount Tai or the Northern Dipper.
Chan Master Fuyan Yan—whose name was Wenyuan—was the son of the Yang family from Xindu County in Chengdu. At the age of eighteen, he relied upon the Guangshou Monastery.
An arrived at ordination and received the full precepts. He traveled to Daci Temple to study the sūtras and śāstras.
After some time, he went to visit Chan Master Zhengfaming and heard the "cloud-gate steamed bun" kōan; upon hearing it, he attained realization.

Seeing that Head Seat Ya possessed noble conduct, he was directed to visit Chan Master Yuanwu of Zhaojue, with whom his spiritual faculties were in profound accord. Thus, he thoroughly penetrated the ultimate matter. When Yuanwu passed away, the Master...

He passed through the frontier pass and first visited Miaoxi at Mount Jing; they attained a particularly deep mutual affinity. Next, he traveled to Mount Nanyue, where he was appointed as the head of the monastic community at Fuyan.
Subsequently, the Governor Gou Long received the command from the Master of Tanzhou to take up residence at Zhidu Monastery, where he propagated the teachings of Yuanwu.

A monk asked, "One shout distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function are simultaneous. Before the monk had finished speaking, the Master shouted. The monk also shouted. The Master shouted twice in succession.

The Master said, "He knows fortune and misfortune. A monk asked, "What is the true master of Dinglin? The Master replied, "He sits and cuts off the tongues of all people under heaven."

(The Master lets out a shout and descends from his seat. He further said: "Spontaneously clear; without deliberation, it is already perfected."
The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future cannot reach this through pointing or instruction; the monks of the world cannot calculate it away nor restrain it.

Above, there is no Buddha or Patriarch to rely upon; below, there is no self to take as a refuge.
