This is the inner meaning. It is not yet the time for formal summer retreat; one must simply cast off body and life over a precipice ten thousand fathoms high.
At such a moment, try to reveal the news. To reach this point, one must be a person of true caliber before it can be attained. Do you understand? This requires calculation.
He could not be found for some time, until he returned of his own accord and said, "I am leaving the seat. Master [Yuan]yan resided at Zhidu Monastery for twelve years before moving to Fuyan.
Disciples flocked to him, and the prosperity of his Dharma assembly was preeminent throughout the Lake and Xiang regions. Right Vice-President Zhang, the Duke of Wei, once remarked:
"Master Yan is sincere and without artifice; his heart and mouth are as one. His practice of the Way is pure and firm, and he becomes even more diligent as he grows older."
He was indeed a model for monastics and an old acquaintance of my own region.

On the twenty-sixth day of the eleventh month of the *pingzi* year of the Shaoxing era, while sitting upright in his chamber, he gathered his elders and entrusted them with his final affairs. He then wrote a verse by hand, saying:
Having attained full maturity through cultivation, he required no further effort; when facing the fray, he was resolute and unyielding—dare anyone dare to challenge him?

To him, the distinction between sage and ordinary, defilement and purity, were like flowers seen before the eyes; he attained mastery over both hell and heaven. With a roar, he threw down his brush and passed away.
His worldly age was sixty-five, and his monastic seniority forty-eight. After cremation, five-colored śarīra relics and sacred bones were enshrined in the monastery’s third life-hall.
Master Ta’s nature was harmonious and easygoing; he lived in accordance with truth and maintained a simple, unadorned lifestyle. The world recognized him as one who propagated the Way.

Regarding the teachings and methods of Yuanwu, he was able to carry on his family tradition. Yet, he remained humble and content with his lot, conducting himself with integrity and refusing to seek profit through pretense.
Those who understood him held him in even greater esteem for these qualities.
Chan Master Huanglong Zhen, whose dharma name was Daozhen, was the son of the Zhao family of Jinling. In his youth, he relied upon Chan Master Baoning Jueyin as a novice.
When Jueyin resided at Puzhao Monastery in Sizhou, he encountered Princess Shuqiao, who selected young novices who maintained the precepts and discipline to bestow the tonsure upon them.

The record states: The Master was among those selected for ordination and received full precepts. After some time, he took leave of Jueyin and went to pay his respects to Chan Master Danxia Chun, from whom he heard the fundamental tenets of the Caodong school.
He subsequently composed a verse which said: "White clouds deeply shroud the ancient, cold crags; Strange herbs and numinous flowers are carried by the colored phoenix.
At midnight, the day is midday; Riding a cow, facing backward, one puts on boots and a robe. When Chun saw this, [he was impressed].
He then traveled elsewhere, journeying through Lake Xiang and arriving at Mount Daimeishan. There he composed a verse on the "Hoe-Planting Well," which says:

"All say the father and son of Mount Daimei are in harmony, yet even as they plant their hoes, they still carry the traces of war. To this day, the single well is like a bright mirror; yet there are times when ripples swirl without a breeze.
Finally, he reached Huanglong, where Master Chan Qing of Caotang saw him and their minds were instantly in accord. From that point on, [Daowei] set aside all other intentions.
In former days, he took up the teachings of the Tripitaka to read them. One evening, hearing the drum for the late evening assembly, he stepped out from the sutra hall;

looking up, he saw the moon and suddenly attained realization. He hurried at once to the abbot’s quarters to present his awakening. Caotang deeply approved of it, and from then on, through diligent practice, he achieved thorough penetration.
At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, when Caotang was avoiding the disturbances by taking refuge at Mount Cao and later moving to Shushan, the Master was with him throughout.

He occupied the first seat and shared his dharma-seat with fellow practitioners. In the fifth year [of his tenure], Provincial Governor and Court Official Cheng of Linchuan commissioned him to take up the abbacy at Caoshan, where he propagated the Way of Cudang. [The monk] was born. The Master struck the meditation seat with his whisk. The monk said, "To refine the ordinary and forge the sage requires profound power;

For a master who possesses the true eye, the nature of the Way remains as it is, and the nature of phenomena (*dharma-tā*) likewise remains as it is. Since the nature of phenomena remains as it is, how could there be any talk of distinctions between self and other? The essential point lies in...
To act according to the occasion—suppressing or elevating, granting or withholding—is merely to remove nails and wedges for others, or to strip away their head-stalls;

this is the ritual for teaching the Dharma in the ancestral Gate of the School. How can it be said that such a person is defined by mere "spiritual bearing"? You have written a letter... [end of fragment].

If you truly desire to uphold the religious teachings, yet harbor this ambition without investigating the mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, then even if you brandish your words with equal vigor, you will only become increasingly estranged from the truth.
Thus, it is not right to fault [Master] Kai for his "Three Mysteries" (Sanxuan);
as for blaming Ba Ling for failing to recognize the "live word," this is simply because you have not yet thoroughly examined my humble writings. Indeed, Ba Ling had personally seen Yunmen...
He was a gatekeeper of the Dharma. While Yunmen was alive, his presence was like that of a king; how could he have been preoccupied with mere words and phrases?
He once said, "If this matter were found within words and phrases, would the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the teachings not themselves consist of words and phrases?
Alas, before even a full turn of the heel had passed, Baling went against his teacher’s instruction, flaunting his own abilities and seeking to win the trust of others.
This means that by employing the "three turns of speech," one is sufficient to answer Yunmen; there is no need to further treat him with excessive caution.

I therefore despise his self-debasement of the ancestral style for the sake of mere verbal phrasing, which subsequently led to the superficial practitioners of later generations boasting in their pursuit of words and phrases.
The loss of the source of the Way began with Ba Ling. Furthermore, how could it ever be said that his words were not "live phrases"?
You showed me your instruction, saying: "When asked about the school of Deva, he replied, 'A non-Buddhist. This can be used as a mirror to see how [others] treat words as dead ones.
If that is so, then when a monk asked De Shan, "What is the Buddha? Shan said, "The Buddha is an old bhikṣu from the Western Heaven. This too should be understood in the same way.
Jian regards this as a "dead phrase. But how could it be so? The Great Function of a Master in responding to the occasion consists simply in awakening beings.

How can it be compared to the study of searching for chapters and picking out phrases, judging them by skill or clumsiness? If one were to take skill itself as the "live phrase," [one would be mistaken].
If "clumsiness" is considered a dead word (*siju*), then Niu-t’ou Feng-ko’s blowing of a cloth-hair was also clumsy; how then could his attendant have attained awakening?
Regarding your discussion of Ba-lung’s three phrases, you say: "To call them 'words' is irrational; yet to call them 'not words' is because they respond to the occasion as living words (*hoju*).
Alas, this misses the mark by a great distance. For although dead words and living words are distinguished within speech, [the distinction lies elsewhere].
There is a distinction between speech that contains speech and speech that is devoid of speech.

Yet, from the perspective of a person of true realization, whether it be a staff, a shout, a rebuke, laughter, anger, or scolding—even the sound of the wind and the dripping of rain, the clarity of dawn and the darkness of dusk—all are nothing other than "live words.
How could they be merely profound sayings or wondrous phrases? One must be like you, responding to the opportune moment with principlelessness; this is what constitutes the live word.
To label such a statement as the "unsurpassed song of the Chan school" implies that the responses of the ancestral masters of old lack any standard or criterion;

they were merely speaking at random according to the occasion, leading people to say their words lack logic, yet if one calls them non-words, they are merely evasive and ambiguous in response to the immediate stimulus.
Alas! Is it appropriate to treat the affairs of the Chan school as a mere game? Furthermore, regarding the scriptures of our own teaching...

The treatise’s great meaning is brilliantly clear; yet the historians still consider that the Chinese people are fond of artifice, and thus they seize upon the words of Zhuangzi and Liezi to bolster its lofty strata, soaring directly above them while remaining unconvinced.
How much more so when you yourself judge the essential purport of our school to be such as this?
Were they to see this, how could they not further increase their disdain and levity? You do not seem to take this into account at all.
What is this? Now, the reason I censured Baling was because he flaunted his phrasing and treated the master-disciple relationship with contempt, thereby failing to grasp the great principle.
You, however, cherish the line "coral branches branch upon branch, supporting the moon.

To censure one for failing to grasp the great principle is to uphold public discourse while correcting its abuses; yet to be mired in a fine phrase and reject public discourse—how will the world regard this?

Is this not so? Thus, it is not that the error of failing to recognize the "live word" (huoju) is unknown; rather, it is because people fail to distinguish between the two kinds of self and do not understand the difficulty with which the Sages formulated their teachings.
It was for this reason that I intended to clarify these matters, as I have already explained in detail within my two replies to Secretariat Vice President Shi.
Indeed, having received the noble models of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, I have set forth this for the sake of scholars in the final age to clearly manifest the fundamental nature.
The fundamental purpose is to cause one to abandon the shadows and lights of daily life and directly realize the original self prior to the kalpa of emptiness.
Because in the present age many take clever rhetoric and profound subtleties as the ultimate standard, two types [of responses] are taught to test the depth of their realization.

Thus, the Tathāgata established the ritual of transformation through the three bodies; Shaolin distinguished between the "skin" and the "marrow" to differentiate the near and the distant; and Dongshan utilized the "partial" and the "correct."
As for the establishment of the fundamental tenets, it was with Maitreya that the single mind was opened into the two gates of True Suchness and Arising-and-Ceasing.
I have therefore employed this teaching to remedy the malady of scholars in the final age who abandon the root. It is not that I am unaware of the difficulty of a sage’s formulation of words.
The verse from the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* cited by you is, in fact, a verse from the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. Furthermore, [the text continues...]
Scholars must clarify the differences between the five periods of the Dharma-wheels (*dharmacakra*). For instance, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* represents the teaching of the third period;
it explains that things are neither empty nor existent, thereby subverting the teaching of emptiness from the second period.

As for the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, it represents the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*) of the fifth period. At that time, the great capacity [of sentient beings] could be awakened; therefore, it was revealed and established for Ānanda.
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Buddha, the statement "That which is called 'true' is not truly true; fearing delusion, I have never openly expounded it" refers to the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*.
It means that when [sentient beings'] faculties were not yet mature in the past, he did not openly expound it; it does not mean that he did not speak it at the time of the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra*.
You, sir, fail to investigate the differences between the five periods [of the Buddha's teaching] and falsely claim that the Sage feared...
I fear the difficulty of establishing definitive teachings. Furthermore, the World-Honored One declared: "I am the Dharma King; I possess mastery over all dharmas.

How could one who is a sovereign Dharma King dare to hesitate in determining truth from falsehood, treating the matter with levity or wavering between two ends, thereby perpetuating confusion for future generations?
Moreover, the various sutras enumerate thousands of practices and myriad methods of the Dharma; how have they ever considered these difficult to master?
"And yet, you leave it unexamined? I recall your esteemed discourse stating: 'Regarding the eighth consciousness—if one says it is real, one fears it lacks intrinsic nature;
if one says it is not real, one fears being deluded into thinking it is annihilated. Therefore, I do not openly expound upon it. Alas!
Every time I reach this passage, I cannot help but set down my scroll in deep regret. Why is this? Because the World-Honored One..."
It says: "The nature of consciousness is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true consciousness. It is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, tranquil and eternally abiding.
Zuoxia then remarked: "Even sages do not dare to consider this as truly real, nor do they dare to consider it as not truly real."
If the World-Honored One were indeed as superficial as this, then where would the sentient beings of the three realms turn for refuge?
Your lifelong practice has been based on falsehood; by reaching this point, your ruin of the spirit is complete.

Now, as for the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, it resolutely and directly points out that the original nature of the one mind is Buddha, which is unlike other teachings. You further claim that there are two kinds of erroneous cultivation, and...
I do not dare to interrupt the flow of his discourse. Lu [Huiyuan] produced two interpretations from a single teaching; however, the World-Honored One was not one who harbored manifold anxieties.
As the Sūtra says: "When I press my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light; when you momentarily raise your mind, the dust of affliction arises first.
This means that the Sage’s wondrously perfect Seed-Wisdom (*gotrajñāna*) is such that there is no application that is not wondrous; it is precisely the sentient beings who harbor anxieties.

It is the deluded mind that clings to objects. I have received the teachings of the Wisdom of All Modes (sarvajñajñāna) and expound the Dharma; yet you, with every step, seek to obstruct and destroy them with deluded thoughts.
Furthermore, your citations of scriptures are neither appropriate nor fitting. Thus, it is not correct to say that you do not understand the Sage’s failure in his choice of words.

Indeed, the proliferation of verbal traces is the source from which heterodox views arise; were it not for the wise and enlightened who receive the words of Righteous Meaning (samyagartha) to refute them, [such views would prevail].

Consequently, as people vie with one another for rebirth, the fundamental path has fallen into decline. I have heard that in the past, during the flourishing era of our school, every individual illuminated the world through their practice of the Way and their moral conduct;
they never sought to be esteemed for establishing written treatises. Yet, when virtue declined, it was then that the *Biographies of Monks* (*Sengzhuan*) first began to be compiled.
Now, you have again introduced a novel approach, recording eulogies and applying praise or censure to conduct. This is [to say the least]...
This is the duty of an author. How could one fail to investigate the essential purport of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*? The *Annals* rectifies the laws of a single king;

it employs expedient means as an auxiliary, uses sincerity to adjudicate ritual propriety, and follows the Way of loyalty to examine human sentiments. It acts according to what is appropriate to rescue from disorder, and adjusts promotions and demotions according to the times—this is its general outline.
I have opened up two kinds of personal regulations to serve as a model for the sublime examples of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, so that students may...
This [approach] sets aside profound understanding to investigate the fundamental; it is what is called "using skillful means to assist function.
To criticize Master Baling Pu for relying on the words and phrases of others is what is called "using sincerity to determine ritual propriety.

To divide the Three Mysteries to reveal the profound significance of the Great Way and thereby rectify abuses is what is called "acting according to suitability to rescue disorder, and promoting or demoting based on the times. All of this is essentially a matter of the mind.
To propagate the Way, one must uphold the great principles of renunciation; if you were to destroy them all, you would fail.
This is what is meant by "evaluating the circumstances based on the principle of loyalty. Your writings, moreover, both deviate from the Way of the Sages and contradict the secular classics;
how can you presume to praise or censure such mad conduct? As for your disparagement of Zhaojue and refusal to accept his "Dead Heart," this too is an extreme violation of propriety.
Even though Chen Shou sought to compile [the Records of the Three Kingdoms] and Ban Gu accepted gold [for the History of the Han], they did not act in such a manner.

When he himself described the *Baoming Sanmei* (Treasure Mirror Samādhi), he claimed it was obtained from an old monk by Zhu Shiying; his own commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra* served to support the words of the *Baoming*.
Yet, when placed within the *Jiufeng Zhuan* (Biographies of Jiufeng), it says: "The stone stele was broken and damaged; there is a wooden stele that records its outline as follows. Alas! This—
It may be said that he closed his eyes and took the gold, as if the market people did not see him; this is also a case of simultaneous suppression.

As for the Treasure Mirror Samādhi (*ratnādarśa-samādhi*), although Dongshan claimed to have received it from Yunyan, it was likely intended as a profound principle for testing people’s intimacy, rather than something to be transmitted as a mere literary document.
Furthermore, the Dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is bestowed universally with an impartial mind, making no distinction even between different species.
How could there have been a fellow student who overheard this and cast a spell to cause the heart of a sage and worthy man to fall ill?
Is it truly so crooked and perverse? Furthermore, his words state: "The double li hexagram has six intersections; the biased and the correct revolve and intermingle. Layered, they become three;

through transformation, they exhaustively become five. Now, Dongshan was one who transmitted the essential tenets of Bodhidharma. As for the hexagram *Chongli* (Double Li), it belongs to Fuxi and Wenwang...

Your Majesty’s letter (if it is indeed as you say, then this would mean that Dongshan’s [Linji] school is transmitting the texts of Fuxi and King Wen; yet, by imitating the Li hexagram, he established the five positions.

But Dongshan was a great master—would he have truly consented to such a thing?). You have brazenly fabricated empty doctrines and slandered the tradition. What punishment should be meted out for such a crime?
Generally speaking, when a matter is obscure regarding reality and harmful to the teachings, even if people do not hold one accountable, how can one escape the scrutiny of the divine spirits?
What? Your Excellency’s criticisms of the ancients have certainly not been few. Yet you yourself have instead rashly sought honor and incurred reproach.
In the past, Xu Jingzong personally participated in the compilation of the Jin History, yet in his later years he fell into the reputation of a sycophant;

consequently, posterity has regarded the Jin History as not having been produced by the hands of upright men, and thus it is not highly esteemed. I hope you will take these former failures as a warning, probe deeply into the source of the Way, and tread upon it with care.
Only after achieving such central rectitude can one leisurely contemplate and, through ritual courtesy, probe the profound depths to compose a code of laws and regulations to bequeath to posterity—
a standard for discerning gain and loss, determining right and wrong, and adjudicated by the Great Mean of the successive sages,

such that for ten thousand generations none shall dare to propose alternative interpretations. As for Bodhidharma’s differentiation of the six schools, I would willingly accept execution at your hands for such a claim.

What more need be said? Since you were unable to do so, I have forced myself to rise once more to scrutinize your fabrications and errors with you, so that future followers of our school shall not tread upon the wreckage of your overturned cart.

This is my lifelong devotion to the Buddha and my resolve to propagate the Way and refute heterodoxy. I have intruded upon your compassionate severity; I humbly pray for your forgiveness of my offense.
